title: Bacterial protein function prediction via multimodal deep learning.
authors: Miklautz, Lukas; Fernandez, Leyden; Muzio, Giulia; Adamer, Michael; Borgwardt, Karsten; Avican, Kemal
abstract: Bacterial proteins are specialized with extensive functional diversity for survival in diverse and stressful environments. A significant portion of these proteins remains functionally uncharacterized, limiting our understanding of bacterial survival mechanisms. Hence, we develop Deep Expression STructure (DeepEST), a multimodal deep learning framework that predicts protein function in bacteria by assigning Gene Ontology (GO) terms. DeepEST comprises two modules: a multi-layer perceptron that uses gene expression and gene location, and a protein structure-based module that uses predicted structures and amino acid sequences. Within DeepEST, we integrate these modules through a learnable weighted linear combination and introduce a novel masked loss function to fine-tune the structure-based predictor for bacterial species. These choices are well suited for bacteria, in which functionally related genes frequently colocalize and are cotranscribed within operons, allowing transcription dynamics to serve as informative, condition-dependent signals. We show that DeepEST outperforms existing protein function prediction methods on a 25-species benchmark, relying solely on amino acid sequence or protein structure. Averaged over the 25 species, DeepEST reaches a protein-centric F (max) of 0.689 and a term-centric micro-AUPRC of 0.756, a relative improvement of 4.4% and 11.6% over the second-best method, the structure-based predictor DeepFRI. Moreover, DeepEST predicts GO terms for unclassified hypothetical proteins across 25 human bacterial pathogens, supporting their experimental characterization. DeepEST bridges organism-specific data integration and structure-based transfer learning, providing a method tailored for bacterial protein function prediction in settings with structural and multi-condition expression data.

title: From prediction to creation: How AI-driven design is reshaping microbial biocatalysis.
authors: Guirimand, Gregory; Mall, Raghvendra; Patel, Chirag; Kudo, Hisashi; Matsuda, Mami; Courdavault, Vincent; Hasunuma, Tomohisa
abstract: Enzyme engineering has long relied on rational design and directed evolution, yet both remain bounded by natural enzyme space - a constraint felt acutely across the largely uncharacterised microbial world. The 2021 advent of accurate structure prediction marked an inflection point, catalysing AI methods that now extend far beyond folding. These tools are organism-agnostic; the microbial domain is their proving ground because it supplies both the uncharacterised sequence space and the expression hosts. Here we examine three stages: mining microbial sequence space; generative design, whether conditioned on structure or sequence; and machine learning-guided directed evolution. We trace the trajectory from reading the protein universe toward writing it, asking where each has delivered for microbial biocatalysis. Because published claims are hard to compare, we propose a tiered framework - catalysis, selectivity, producibility, process fit - for judging whether an AI-designed enzyme is a useful biocatalyst rather than merely a functional protein.

title: Elucidating the gel-enhancing mechanism of ferulic acid with myofibrillar protein: Insights from molecular docking and dynamics simulations on water-holding capacity and network formation.
authors: Chang, Haijun; Huang, Yu; Wen, Xin; Hu, Yu; Zhou, Wenbin; Wu, Li
abstract: The purpose of this study is to elucidate the mechanism of interaction and the effects of ferulic acid (FA) on myofibrillar proteins (MPs), as well as its impact on protein properties and gel characteristics. Fluorescence quenching of MPs by FA was demonstrated to occur via a static mechanism, as evidenced by integrated fluorescence spectroscopy, receptor-ligand docking, computational molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and physicochemical assays. The FA-MP complex is primarily stabilized by hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic forces, resulting in a tighter protein conformation. These interactions significantly enhanced protein solubility, reduced surface hydrophobicity and particle size, and effectively suppressed protein aggregation. The application of FA at a concentration of 0.4 mmol/L facilitated the formation of a homogeneous and compact three-dimensional gel network, which in turn led to enhanced water retention, improved viscoelasticity, and more uniform water distribution. Correlation analysis further corroborated the relationships between physicochemical properties of the protein and gel quality. These studies elucidate the mechanism of interaction between FA and MPs at the molecular level and lay the foundation for the use of FA as a native functional ingredient in the production of higher-quality meats with enhanced nutritional value.

title: Integrative structural glycobiology: From molecular recognition to dynamic multivalent assemblies.
authors: Perez, Serge
abstract: Protein-carbohydrate recognition plays an important role in structural biology. Glycans store molecular information through their monosaccharide makeup, stereochemistry, linkage positions, branching, substitutions, and three-dimensional shapes. Glycans are often flexible and structurally diverse, and their interactions are typically individually weak. As a result, glycan recognition in biology usually cannot be described as a single, static ligand fitting into a protein binding pocket. Instead, it depends on a mix of factors, including glycan shape, protein structure, hydration, electrostatic forces, molecular movement, context, density, and multivalency. These factors have led structural glycobiology to shift from focusing only on isolated high-resolution structures to using both experimental and computational data to build models that span different spaces and times. This review examines the main ideas behind this shift. It highlights what makes carbohydrate recognition different from other ligand-protein interactions. It offers a practical, evidence-based way to interpret structural models.

title: Structure of the Chimalliviridae bacteriophage Goslar reveals host recognition and infection machinery.
authors: Basu, Dwaipayan; Gu, Yajie; Li, Ying-Xing; Forman, Taylor; Ghassemian, Majid; Min, Ryan K; Pogliano, Joe; Corbett, Kevin D
abstract: Large-genome bacteriophages (phages) of the Chimalliviridae family have a distinctive life cycle, building compartments inside infected bacterial cells that broadly protect their genomes from host defenses. Here, we use cryo-electron microscopy to determine a structure of the Escherichia coli-infecting Chimalliviridae phage Goslar. We combine manual modeling of 25 structural proteins with AlphaFold structure predictions of an additional three proteins to generate a composite model with 2888 protein chains from 28 different structural proteins, totaling more than 1.4 million amino acid residues. Our structure reveals the architecture of the Goslar capsid, portal, tail, and baseplate, highlighting structural similarities and differences with other tailed phages. Combining our structural data with quantitative mass spectrometry of Goslar virions, we identify several high-copy virion-associated proteins that likely play key roles when injected into host cells upon infection. We also identify a Chimalliviridae-specific family of proteins that form long, flexible filaments anchored at the phage baseplate and which incorporate carbohydrate-binding domains, suggesting a key role in host recognition.

title: Mutation-induced structural and dynamic perturbations at the IL-17A-IL-17RA interface: Therapeutic insights from multi-replicate molecular dynamics simulations.
authors: Razzaq, Afsheen; Sardar, Madiha; Mushtaq, Mamona; Nur-E-Alam, Mohammad; Ghayur, Muhammad Nabeel; Ul-Haq, Zaheer
abstract: The interaction between Interleukin-17A (IL-17A) and its receptor IL-17RA plays a key role in pro-inflammatory signal transduction and is implicated in the pathogenesis of inflammatory autoimmune diseases. Blocking this protein-protein interaction is a major approach to developing therapeutic agents to inhibit IL-17A-induced signaling. Predicting the consequences of mutations on structure and function in proteins can be accomplished by using computational methods, which are relatively inexpensive and rapid compared with experimental methods. Here, we used a multidimensional in silico approach to gain insight into the functional and thermodynamic consequences of targeted mutation of hotspot residues of IL-17A. The focus of our analysis was on the residues in the two chains that are equivalent to hotspot residues of the related cytokine, IL-17F, at positions 55 and 67 of chain B and 85 and 86 of chain A. Comprehensive analysis of the conformational dynamics, interaction profiles, and structural transitions of the four mutant variant systems (R55V, W67V, Y85I, and H86S) and the wild-type system was performed based on molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and Molecular Mechanics/Generalized Born Surface Area (MM/GBSA) calculations. A total of 3 mus simulations were performed: three 200 ns replicates for each of the wild-type and mutant complexes. Results from principal component analysis (PCA) and free energy landscape (FEL) analyses indicate conformational destabilization of the mutant systems. These findings help to elucidate the mechanisms of molecular interactions involved in the dynamics of cytokine-receptor interaction. Changes in these important PSN network parameters resulted in differences in hub connectivity and distribution of the links between the systems, which suggests allosteric perturbations and remodeling of the system in the interaction between IL-17A and IL-17RA when compared to the wild-type systems. The multiple-replica MD simulation protocol provided insight into how mutations affected the structure, contact networks, dynamics, and binding affinity of the IL-17A/IL-17RA complex, shedding light on the IL-17A downstream signaling cascades. Overall, this study provides a fundamental framework for designing therapeutic strategies to regulate IL-17A-mediated inflammatory diseases.

title: Structural insights into West Nile virus programmed ribosomal frameshifting reveal coordinated regulation by RNA, ribosome, and nascent peptide.
authors: Wu, Mingbo; Zhou, Haolong; Jin, Qianqian; Wang, Yue; Yuan, Shuai
abstract: Programmed -1 ribosomal frameshifting (-1 PRF) is essential for West Nile virus (WNV) gene expression and generates NS1', a protein implicated in viral replication and pathogenesis. However, the structural pathway by which translating ribosomes traverse the WNV frameshift signal remains poorly understood. Here, we combined cryo-electron microscopy, RNA structural modeling, molecular dynamics simulations, and functional analyses to investigate the mechanism of WNV -1 PRF. We resolved a pre-frameshift ribosomal complex together with four translocation intermediates, including a previously uncharacterized semi-rotated state in which the 40S subunit undergoes partial rotation while tRNAs remain in near-canonical A/A-P/P configurations. This intermediate is accompanied by remodeling of conserved peptidyl-transferase-center nucleotides, suggesting that active-site rearrangements can precede canonical tRNA movement during translocation. Structural modeling and simulations further suggest that the WNV frameshift-stimulatory RNA exists as a compact but conformationally heterogeneous ensemble capable of adopting multiple stable or metastable pseudoknot architectures. In addition, we identified direct interactions between the nascent viral peptide and the ribosomal exit tunnel, and disruption of the tunnel-occupying peptide reduced frameshifting efficiency. Together, our findings suggest that WNV frameshifting is governed not by a single stimulatory element but by the coordinated coupling of RNA dynamics, ribosome remodeling, and nascent-chain interactions.IMPORTANCEViruses often rely on a process called programmed ribosomal frameshifting to produce proteins important for infection. West Nile virus (WNV), a mosquito-borne pathogen that can cause severe neurological disease in humans, uses this strategy to generate NS1', a protein linked to viral replication and pathogenesis. However, how ribosomes are redirected into an alternative reading frame remains incompletely understood. Here, we provide structural insights into ribosome movement during translation of the WNV frameshift signal. Our findings also suggest that the viral RNA can adopt alternative conformations and that the emerging viral peptide may influence frameshifting efficiency. Together, these observations contribute to our understanding of how RNA structure, ribosomal dynamics, and nascent peptides may influence viral protein expression.

title: Replicate-resolved pressure-cooling responses of tobacco mosaic virus coat protein reveal robust volumetric changes and non-dominant conformational redistribution.
authors: Bonafe, Carlos Francisco Sampaio; Teixeira, Juan Philippe; Cesar de Melo Freire, Caio; Bajay, Miklos Maximiliano; de Lima Neto, Daniel Ferreira
abstract: High hydrostatic pressure can alter protein structure through changes in system volume, hydration, packing, and conformational sampling. We combined a sequential pressure and pressure-cooling molecular-dynamics pathway for tobacco mosaic virus coat protein (TMVcp) with replicate-resolved analysis of Native (1 bar, 300 K), high hydrostatic pressure (HHP; 2500 bar, 300 K), and HHP plus low temperature (HHP+LT; 2500 bar, 255 K). Three independently velocity-initialised 20 ns replicates were analysed per condition after discarding the first 200 ps, yielding 89,109 frames. Relative to Native, mean box volume decreased by 9.15% under HHP and 11.49% under HHP+LT, while density increased by 10.07% and 12.98%. Water occupancy within 0.35 nm increased by 10.73% and 18.45%, respectively; after normalization for bulk densification, the residual increase was near-null for HHP (+0.6%) but persisted for HHP+LT (+4.9%). In pooled Cartesian PCA, PC1-PC2 captured 38.5% of total variance but did not separate same-condition from across-condition replicate pairs (Jensen-Shannon divergence 0.771 versus 0.768; p = 0.476). Condition-associated signal instead concentrated in PC3-PC4, with mean divergence of 0.545 within conditions and 0.773 across conditions; selection-aware exact permutation retained significance (p = 0.0143). Pairwise C-alpha RMSD and backbone-dihedral PCA supported condition-associated differences, although first-half versus second-half divergences indicated incomplete convergence. Endpoint epitope comparisons showed residue-level enrichment for Native and HHP+LT, but not HHP. Overall, TMVcp exhibited robust volumetric responses, condition-dependent near-protein hydration, and reproducible but non-dominant conformational redistribution without implying equilibrium convergence or causal antibody remodelling. These findings distinguish pressure-driven densification from cooling-associated local hydration effects while preserving appropriate mechanistic caution.

title: HydroGuard: a controlled release hydrogel-phage delivery system to combat catheter-associated urinary tract infections.
authors: Rao, Shilpa; McLean, Rhyan; Zakir Hussain, Aadila
abstract: Catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs) rank as the fourth-most significant nosocomial infection globally. CAUTIs account for approximately 80% of hospital-acquired urinary tract infections and represent nearly one-third of all device-associated infections. Urinary catheters serve as a hub for bacteria to form highly resistant biofilms containing pathogens, like Enterococcus (E.) faecalis that reduce effectiveness of the immune system and antibiotic treatments. Therefore, tackling biofilm formation at the catheter surface becomes a crucial step in mitigating CAUTIs. We aim to address E. faecalis biofilm formation by engineering HydroGuard: a Gelatin Methacryloyl (Gel-MA)-based hydrogel injected with bacteriophages, to provide targeted, enzyme-triggered antimicrobial activity. Enterococcus faecalis expresses gelatinase (GelE), a zinc metalloprotease that enhances biofilm formation. GelMA is susceptible to GelE-mediated degradation, enabling enzyme-triggered release of bacteriophages that specifically lyse E. faecalis. For a Biosafety Level 1 proof-of-concept experiment with a well-studied host and phage system, we heterologously expressed GelE in Escherichia (E.) coli DH5alpha to emulate native E. faecalis expression. This system was tested on dynamically grown biofilms, to simulate similar conditions to the urinary tract. Currently, the E. coli system has shown preliminary inhibition when tested against the hydrogel product, however testing of different phage combinations is needed. Mathematical modelling identified hydrogel crosslinking density as a critical tuneable parameter governing therapeutic availability and predicted nonlinear, degradation-dependent phage release profiles. Sensitivity analyses revealed design trade-offs between structural stability and antimicrobial responsiveness. Together, the biofilm, hydrogel, phage-bacteria, and protein design models form a multiscale computational framework that links biofilm development and environmental conditions to enzyme-mediated hydrogel degradation, phage release, and bacterial suppression. Agent-based biofilm simulations captured emergent spatial dynamics under nutrient, flow, and pH constraints, while a coupled predator-prey model investigated phage-bacteria population dynamics within the degrading GelMA matrix. Computational protein design further explored collagen-like peptide motifs with enhanced folding stability and preserved gelatinase cleavage sites, providing a molecular-level approach to tuneable degradation kinetics. This multiscale framework provides predictive insight into how biofilm conditions, hydrogel degradation, and phage availability interact within the proposed system, while the preliminary experimental observations provide supporting evidence for its feasibility. By integrating synthetic biology, tissue engineering, and modelling, HydroGuard offers a novel, non-antibiotic strategy for CAUTI prevention.

title: Site Specific Hydration Contributes to the Thermal Stability of Proteins and Protein-Complexes.
authors: Rider, Robert L; Xi, Zhenyu; Hillaire, Adam; Powell, Joanna; Spelbring, Amy; Evans, Kacie; Lantz, Carter; Scott, Elena; Barondeau, David; Raab, Shannon; Clemmer, David; Laganowsky, Arthur; Russell, David H
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Water is integral to protein structure and stability, yet ensemble measurements rarely identify the hydration interactions associated with stabilization. Here, variable-temperature electrospray ionization ion mobility mass spectrometry, conformation-resolved thermodynamic analysis, and molecular dynamics simulations are combined to examine solvent-dependent thermal stability of chymotrypsin inhibitor 2 (CI-2), a model two-state folder, and the barnase-barstar (Bn-B*) complex, which contains a highly polar binding interface. Replacing H (2) O with D (2) O raises the thermal transition temperature of both systems by approximately 3  degrees C, favors compact conformations, and reduces the relative thermodynamic accessibility of extended states. The conformationally resolved enthalpy-entropy compensation reveals D (2) O increases enthalpy for CI-2 but reduces enthalpy for Bn-B* as a result of opposing effects on the individual subunits of the complex. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that lower solvent-accessible surface areas and fewer protein-water hydrogen bonds in D (2) O coexist with longer water residence times at specific structural sites. In CI-2, the strongest changes localize to the second beta-strand/C-terminal region; in Bn-B*, persistent hydration is concentrated at the charged protein-protein interface. Together, these results support a model in which D (2) O dependent stabilization is associated not only with the extent of hydration, but the site and lifetime of water interactions. More broadly, this work provides an experimental framework for resolving solvent-dependent conformational thermodynamics of protein unfolding and interactions, enabling direct comparison of free-energy landscapes across solution environments.

title: PHENOMS: Open-Source Software for Rust-Accelerated Hydrogen-Bond Analysis in Molecular Dynamics Simulations.
authors: Novy, Brandon; Lin, Shu-Hang; Dey, Rishabh; Temple, Brenda; Hajicek, Nicole; Petrotchenko, Evgeniy V; Borchers, Christoph H; Sondek, John; Popov, Konstantin I
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) provides powerful insight into protein structure and dynamics, but interpretation of protection patterns at atomic resolution often requires complementary computational modeling. We present PHENOMS, an open-source Python package that integrates molecular dynamics trajectories with HDX-MS data to analyze backbone hydrogen-bond networks by tracking how individual hydrogen bonds and residue-residue contacts form, break, and reorganize throughout the simulations. This residue-level analysis can reveal local structural changes that may be missed by conventional global trajectory metrics. PHENOMS employs a multithreaded, Rust-accelerated computational engine that achieved an average 16-fold speedup (up to 100-fold) over widely used Python-based MD analysis packages in our benchmarks, while retaining individual hydrogen-bond resolution in every trajectory frame. We demonstrate PHENOMS through multiple retrospective case studies using published and in-house datasets, showing that it can recapitulate HDX-MS protection patterns, identify key residues that drive coordinated structural changes, and benchmark the computational efficiency of the approach. With automated quality-control workflows, PHENOMS provides a framework for integrating hydrogen-bond analysis with HDX-MS data or serves as a standalone, high-throughput tool for analyzing MD trajectories for broader applications in protein engineering, drug discovery, and structural biology.

title: A multispecies foundation model for genome function prediction, gene annotation and sequence design.
authors: Boshar, Sam; Evans, Benjamin; Tang, Ziqi; Adel, Yanis; Bornachot, Yohan; Sidbon, Shawn; Lorbeer, Franziska K; Picard, Armand; Rajesh, Chandana; Seitz, Evan; Emms, David; Mendoza-Revilla, Javier; Hernandez, Ariana; Al-Ani, Fatimah; Karch, Tristan; Schiff, Yair; Lopez, Marie; Laterre, Alexandre; Beguir, Karim; Koo, Peter; Kuleshov, Volodymyr; Stark, Alexander; de Almeida, Bernardo P; Pierrot, Thomas
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Comparative genomics and synthetic biology require models that can interpret, annotate, and design DNA sequences across species, yet genomic models have not combined these capabilities beyond a few well-characterized organisms. Here we introduce Nucleotide Transformer v3 (NTv3), a long-context cross-kingdom foundation model that provides a common backbone for functional prediction, gene annotation and controllable sequence generation across phylogenetically diverse species. NTv3 is pretrained on more than 128,000 genomes using sequences up to 1 Mb and post-trained on 16,262 functional tracks across 15 animal and plant genomes. NTv3 performs comparably to AlphaGenome on matched human assays and matches or exceeds evaluated published models for functional-track prediction across 19 species spanning mammals, birds, fish, plants, fungi and protists. Ablation experiments show that both genome pre-training and expanding functional supervision from human and mouse to 15 species improve track prediction. Leveraging these learned functional representations, NTv3 outperforms leading ab initio gene predictors across mammals, plants and insects, with fewer spurious gene models and improved recovery and reduced fragmentation of long genes. Finally, the same representations can be used with discrete diffusion to design regulatory DNA sequences with specific activity levels. We demonstrate this in plant and fly promoters and enhancers, and experimentally validate the activity and promoter selectivity of the generated fly enhancers. Together, NTv3 unifies genome interpretation, gene annotation and regulatory sequence design across the animal and plant kingdoms, with direct relevance to agriculture, biodiversity research and biotechnology.

title: Generative design of functional disordered regions in a developmental transcription factor.
authors: Denes, Lance; Emenecker, Ryan J; Wang, Nongyun; Chirumamilla, Devi; Mohotti, Rashmi; Holehouse, Alex S; Holt, Liam; Lionnet, Timothee
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Rapid advances in protein structure design have not translated to intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). This is largely due to our incomplete understanding of how IDR sequence encodes function. Here, we use stem cell differentiation as a model to map functional sequence features in the C-terminal IDR of the transcription factor RUNX2, which is required to bind chromatin and regulate gene expression during osteogenesis. Surprisingly, linear IDR motifs are dispensable; instead, the conformational dynamics of the IDR predict function. We develop an algorithm for rational IDR design based on biophysical principles, and use it to generate functional IDRs de novo . These findings extend generative protein design beyond the folded proteome.

title: Comprehensive assessment of disordered linker predictions using data from the third critical assessment of protein intrinsic disorder.
authors: Zhao, Bi; Yu, Jing; Kurgan, Lukasz
journal: Protein science : a publication of the Protein Society
abstract: Disordered flexible linkers (DFLs) are an abundant type of intrinsically disordered regions that contribute to many cellular functions by facilitating movement between adjacent functional domains. Several new sequence-based predictors of DFL regions have been published in recent years, prompting the need to evaluate their predictive performance comparatively. We used the recently released data from the third Critical Assessment of protein Intrinsic Disorder prediction (CAID3) to comprehensively evaluate nine DFL predictors, including seven methods that participated in CAID3 and two additional, recently published DFL predictors. We expanded the CAID3 evaluation by examining predictions on a larger dataset and, arguably, more practical test scenarios that assess predictions at the residue, region, and protein levels. We also evaluated on a subset of CAID3 proteins that share less than 30% sequence similarity with the training sets of the included DFL predictors, yielding more robust estimates of predictive performance. We showed that several DFL predictors accurately identify DFL residues among other types of disordered residues. We also found that different methods perform better in different scenarios, with several methods producing very accurate predictions of DFL residues and a few performing well when predicting proteins with DFLs. While our results suggest that progress has been made in recent years, driven by the use of deep learning and protein language models, we also identified a major weakness in current tools, as they are unable to reproduce the correct sizes and numbers of DFL regions. We also suggested several ways to develop new DFL predictors that would address this issue.

title: Phyfold: environment aware mathematical modeling for protein folding dynamics integrated with physics informed neural network.
authors: Ul Rahman, Jamshaid; Noureen, Iqra; Mannan, Abdul; Uwitije, Rongin
abstract: Protein folding remains a fundamental problem in computational biology, where understanding folding trajectories and dynamic behavior under physiological conditions is critical for linking structure to function. Recent advances such as AlphaFold have revolutionized sequence to structure prediction, establishing a powerful and robust foundation for computational protein modeling. Building upon this success, we introduce a novel physics informed computational framework that expands static structure prediction toward dynamic and physically consistent modeling of protein folding processes. The proposed framework unifies a mathematically grounded reaction diffusion model of folding kinetics with deep sequence embeddings through a physics informed neural network (PINN), ensuring consistency with governing physical laws while remaining biologically grounded. We refer to this unified framework as PhyFold. Our results illustrate that the proposed approach effectively captures environment dependent folding dynamics and shows strong agreement with both numerical reference solutions and experimental fluorescence measurements under physiologically relevant conditions. By explicitly integrating environmental factors such as temperature, pressure, and pH, PhyFold enables realistic, physics aware simulation of protein folding dynamics. This approach offers a natural extension of modern structure prediction methods and opens new directions for protein design, structure guided drug discovery, and personalized medicine. The code to reproduce the work is available at https://github.com/jamshaidwarraich/PhyFold.git .Scientific contributionPhyFold introduces a hybrid Bio-Physics Informed Neural Network framework that models protein folding kinetics as a reaction diffusion partial differential equation with environmentally modulated kinetic coefficients, integrated with ProtT5 sequence embeddings for sequence specific spatiotemporal prediction an approach not previously demonstrated in the literature. Unlike purely data driven or static structure prediction methods, PhyFold explicitly encodes temperature, pH, and pressure dependence into governing kinetic coefficients, enabling physically interpretable simulation of cooperative folding transitions across diverse physiological conditions. Dual validation against finite difference reference solutions and experimental GFP fluorescence measurements confirms mathematical consistency and biological relevance, establishing PhyFold as a computationally efficient surrogate for environment aware protein folding dynamics.

title: ECOD in 2027: a modernized interface and an updated classification of protein domains.
authors: Schaeffer, R Dustin; Roy, Barsha; Guo, Rui; Cong, Qian; Medvedev, Kirill E; Grishin, Nick V
abstract: The Evolutionary Classification of Domains (ECOD) organizes protein domains into a hierarchy of evolutionary relationships, encompassing both experimentally determined and computationally predicted structures. ECOD now classifies 2.9M domains, of which  approximately 1.37M derived from the Protein Data Bank and 1.51M from predicted models in the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database. The principal development we report here is a complete rebuild of the ECOD web resource. Search has been reconstructed around three modalities: (i) sequence, (ii) structure, and (iii) keyword. Foldseek now is the primary search method for the ECOD web page, searching a  approximately 457k representative domain database that is also distributed for local use. Results are presented through a Mol* interactive viewer, and a new API has been developed for programmatic access to the database. Alongside the interface, the pipeline for classifying new PDB entries has been rebuilt and returned to a regular cadence, family groups have been synchronized with Pfam v38.2, the bulk distributables have been reorganized and now include the search databases, the ligands in contact with each domain are recorded for experimental structures and annotated with drug cross-references from DrugDomain, and a registry has been introduced through which ECOD assigns stable identifiers to gene-called proteins and records the structures it predicts. ECOD is freely available at http://prodata.swmed.edu/ecod.

title: One pocket, two poses: How sequence context shapes non-additive binding.
authors: Rao, Jingyou; Coyote-Maestas, Willow
abstract: In a recent issue, Jiang et al.(1) combine combinatorial mutagenesis, reference-independent epistasis analysis, binding measurements, NMR, and molecular dynamics to show how specific peptide conformations and PIN1 residues generate non-additive recognition, directly linking statistical epistasis to concrete molecular mechanisms across a complete sequence landscape.

title: Characterization and domain dissection of a PL39 alginate lyase algtm3 from the marine thermophile Rhodothermus profundi.
authors: Yu, Jiaqing; Kong, Ruimin; Guo, Jingyue; Fu, Ruixuan; Bin, Yiqing; Li, Wei; Ren, Yao; Ge, Fanglan
abstract: Alginate lyases are important biocatalysts for the preparation of bioactive alginate oligosaccharides from brown algae. However, the application of currently available alginate lyases is often constrained by insufficient thermostability and catalytic efficiency. In this study, a PL39 family alginate lyase, designated Algtm3, was identified from the thermophilic deep-sea bacterium Rhodothermus profundi (type strain PRI 2902ᵀ = DSM 22212ᵀ = JCM 15944ᵀ) through genome mining, heterologously expressed in Escherichia coli, and systematically characterized. Algtm3 exhibited optimal activity at 70  degrees C and pH 8.0, and retained more than 90% of its initial activity after incubation at 65  degrees C for 60 min, indicating excellent thermal stability. Domain truncation analysis revealed that the Chondroitin AC/alginate lyase superfamily domain and the Hepar_II_III catalytic domain are essential for maintaining proper protein folding, soluble production, and catalytic activity. In contrast, deletion of the C-terminal T9SS sorting domain improved enzyme performance in the heterologous expression system, with the truncated variant Algtm3dc exhibiting a 1.98-fold higher activity than the wild-type enzyme. Structural modeling and molecular docking analyses suggested that C-terminal truncation preserved the catalytic core while inducing local changes in the substrate-binding region, which may contribute to enhanced catalytic efficiency. TLC and ESI-MS analyses demonstrated that Algtm3 could degrade sodium alginate, polyM, and polyG, producing alginate oligosaccharides mainly with degrees of polymerization ranging from 1 to 4, and exhibited both endolytic and exolytic degradation characteristics. Collectively, these findings provide insights into the domain organization and structure-function relationship of PL39 family alginate lyases and highlight the potential of Algtm3 as a thermostable biocatalyst for the efficient production of functional alginate oligosaccharides.

title: An educational activity tailored for undergraduate students on AI-driven nanobody design for targeted antiviral therapeutics.
authors: Idris, Adi; Idres, Yusuf M; Bhattacharjee, Kamanasish; Gao, Wenqing
abstract: Protein-based biologics are converging at an unprecedented pace as generative artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes early-stage drug discovery. Nanobodies, single-domain antibody fragments derived from camelid heavy chain-only immunoglobulins, are an emerging class of antiviral biologics prized for their small size, stability, and access to cryptic viral epitopes. Traditional nanobody discovery relies on animal immunization and phage display screening, a process that can take 6 to 12 months and is entirely inaccessible within a standard undergraduate laboratory session. Here, we describe a succinct, in silico-based laboratory activity that uses a generative AI protein design server, GeoFlow-V3 (https://prot.design/), to allow undergraduate students to design a novel antiviral nanobody against the influenza A virus (IAV) hemagglutinin (HA) protein. This activity builds on our group's prior use of generative AI for undergraduate siRNA design teaching and extends the same pedagogical model to structural protein engineering. To our knowledge, this is the first use of a generative AI protein design platform for teaching nanobody design at the undergraduate level.

title: Reaction Mechanism and Chemoselectivity of an Enzymatic PAS Domain: A Combined MD and QM/MM Study.
authors: Xiang, Sijie; Sheng, Xiang; Su, Hao
journal: The journal of physical chemistry. B
abstract: A Per-ARNT-Sim (PAS) domain exhibits oxidative N-demethylation activity toward dimethylamine (DMA); however, the detailed reaction mechanism remains elusive, thus hindering the rational engineering of the enzyme. In this work, we conducted molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and quantum mechanical/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) calculations to investigate the PAS domain-catalyzed DMA N-demethylation reaction. Our results indicate that the protonated substrate DMA is the most plausible proton donor during the formation of compound I (Cpd I, iron(IV)-oxo porphyrin cation radical). The calculated energy barrier for Cpd I generation is 14.4 kcal/mol, which is the rate-determining step of the reaction. Following its generation, Cpd I can rapidly oxidize the substrate via an electron-transfer-initiated hydrogen atom abstraction. The chemoselectivity favoring methyl hydroxylation over amine oxidation is mainly determined by the protein environment. Our computations provide mechanistic insights into the heme-dependent oxidative N-demethylase (HODM)-catalyzed reaction and offer information for the rational design of new PAS enzymes.

title: Poised for Allostery: Specific Interactions Underlie Precise Positioning of the C-Terminal Tail in Phosphofructokinase-1.
authors: Khodam Hazrati, Mehrnoosh; Nguyen, Truong-An; Timr, Stepan
journal: The journal of physical chemistry. B
abstract: Disordered terminal segments often regulate enzymes, but how such flexible elements achieve the spatial precision required for allostery remains poorly understood. Using human phosphofructokinase-1 as a model system, we combine enhanced-sampling molecular dynamics simulations, conservation-guided spatial analysis, prior allosteric network analysis, and coarse-grained modeling to show that allosteric positioning of the C-terminal tail, defined by residue-level contacts with the catalytic and regulatory domains, is maintained by a few key hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interactions. This positioning enables the conserved tail residues L766 and E767 to dynamically couple the tail to the active site through a conserved surface region and to bridge the catalytic and regulatory domains in the T-state, experimentally associated with ATP inhibition. In contrast, coarse-grained simulations lacking explicit directional representation of hydrogen-bonding interactions fail to maintain stable tail docking, whereas including selected OLIVES-derived native hydrogen-bond terms improves the stability of the T-state-like docking pose. These findings support sequence-specific surface docking of a disordered enzyme tail as a physicochemical mechanism for allosteric regulation.

title: Hesperetin Inhibits Abeta Early Aggregation by Disrupting the Continuity of the beta-Sheet Structure.
authors: Zhang, Yu; Wu, Yelong; Zhang, Shengli; Zhang, Lei; Li, Xuhua
journal: The journal of physical chemistry. B
abstract: The misfolding and pathological aggregation of amyloid-beta (Abeta) into insoluble amyloid deposits are closely associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD). Inhibiting early Abeta assembly is a critical strategy for the development of antiamyloid therapeutics. Hesperetin (HST), a natural flavanone abundant in citrus fruits, has been reported to inhibit Abeta fibrillogenesis and reduce Abeta-associated cytotoxicity. However, the molecular mechanism underlying HST-mediated inhibition of Abeta aggregation remains unclear. In particular, whether HST acts through mechanisms similar to other natural compounds or employs a distinct inhibitory strategy is yet to be determined. Here, we employed replica exchange molecular dynamics (REMD) simulations to investigate how HST modulates Abeta early aggregation and beta-sheet assembly at the atomic level. The results demonstrate that HST disrupts the continuity of beta-sheet structures within Abeta dimers, as evidenced by restricted beta-strand extension. Mechanistically, HST preferentially interacts with aggregation-prone regions of Abeta through a synergistic interaction network of hydrogen-bonding, hydrophobic, pi-pi stacking, and cation-pi interactions. Notably, HST-mediated hydrogen bonding with the Abeta backbone perturbs the local hydrogen-bonding environment required for beta-sheet extension, while cooperative nonpolar and aromatic interactions further stabilize HST-bound conformations and weaken intra- and intermolecular interaction networks involved in Abeta self-assembly. Collectively, these findings reveal a specific mechanism by which HST regulates Abeta aggregation through disruption of beta-sheet continuity, which provides atomic-level insights into the antiamyloid activity of natural flavanones.

title: Histidine Tautomerism-Mediated Regulation of beta-Hairpin Formation and Primary Nucleation in Amyloidogenic PrP(106-126) A117 V Peptides.
authors: Wang, Lisha; Li, Jing; Altayib, Ahmed; Zhu, Rongrong; Sun, Yue; Shi, Hu; Gao, Lizhen
journal: The journal of physical chemistry. B
abstract: Histidine tautomerism is increasingly recognized as a subtle yet powerful regulator of protein structural dynamics, yet its mechanistic role in amyloid nucleation remains poorly understood. In current study, we investigate how histidine protonation states govern the early stage aggregation and primary nucleation of PrP(106-126) A117 V, a prion-related peptide whose mutation markedly accelerates oligomer formation and cytotoxicity. Using molecular dynamics simulations, we systematically characterized the conformational ensembles of monomers through tetramers across distinct histidine tautomeric states (delta and epsilon). We find that tautomerism exerts minimal influence on beta-sheet propensity in monomers and dimers, but becomes decisive at the trimer and tetramer level: the (deltadeltaepsilon) trimer adopts a beta-hairpin, while the (deltaepsilonepsilonepsilon) tetramer harbors two beta-hairpins that collectively define a nascent nucleation core. Based on these observations, we hypothesize a potential two-step nucleation mechanism within the primary nucleation stage, in which structurally heterogeneous intermediates first accumulate, and one beta-hairpin then serves as a template to recruit and organize a second, culminating in a beta-hairpin-enriched nucleus. Our results establish histidine tautomerism as a molecular switch that gates the transition from disordered oligomers to ordered nuclei, offering a physicochemical framework for understanding primary nucleation in prion and, more broadly, amyloidogenic systems.

title: FE65 Recognition Rewires the Dynamic Contact Network of the Amyloid Precursor Protein Intracellular Domain.
authors: Mandal, Nabanita; Skepo, Marie
journal: The journal of physical chemistry. B
abstract: The amyloid precursor protein intracellular domain (AICD) is a short, intrinsically disordered signaling fragment that mediates interactions with adaptor proteins involved in APP trafficking and transcription-associated regulation. Among these partners, FE65 recognizes the conserved YENPTY-containing region of AICD, yet the ensemble-level mechanism underlying this interaction remains unclear. Here, we use molecular dynamics simulations to compare unbound and bound AICD together with YENPTY-motif mutant variants. In the unbound state, AICD samples a heterogeneous conformational ensemble dominated by disordered states while retaining transient local structure and recurrent intramolecular contacts. Upon FE65 binding, AICD does not collapse into a single rigid conformation; instead, its conformational ensemble is redistributed toward interaction-compatible substates. Residue-resolved contact analyses identify localized interaction hotspots within and adjacent to the YENPTY region, including aromatic and polar residues that dominate the bound-state contact network. Mutations within the YENPTY motif alter the balance between compact and extended conformations while preserving the intrinsically disordered character of the peptide. Together, these results support a recognition mechanism in which FE65 binds a partially organized AICD ensemble via localized interaction hotspots and ensemble reweighting, rather than through complete disorder-to-order folding. This work provides a molecular framework for understanding APP intracellular-tail recognition and its regulation by sequence-localized perturbations. More broadly, these findings illustrate how intrinsically disordered motifs can achieve specific molecular recognition through redistribution of dynamic contact networks without undergoing complete disorder-to-order transitions.

title: Coiled Coils as a Programmable Platform for Computational Biosensor Design.
authors: Kluge, Paul; Shabani, Faezeh; Gemming, Sibylle; Kunze, Georg
journal: Chembiochem : a European journal of chemical biology
abstract: Coiled coils are a versatile class of alpha-helical protein motifs characterized by recurring sequence patterns that direct their assembly into defined oligomeric bundles and underpin a wide range of biological functions. The well-established sequence-structure relationships governing coiled-coil formation enable predictive control over stability, specificity, and oligomerization state, making them attractive and chemically tractable building blocks for biosensor design in applications ranging from single-molecule detection to synthetic biochemical circuits and functional nanomaterials. After revisiting the theoretical foundations of coiled-coil architecture, this review outlines strategies to engineer programmable binding interfaces that can be rationally tuned to generate orthogonal, high-affinity interaction pairs, enabling flexible and modular biosensor platforms. Particular emphasis is placed on recent advances in computational and data-driven design approaches, including machine-learning and AI-based strategies, alongside established rational and empirical methods for coiled-coil construction. These complementary design principles underpin the development of coiled-coil-based biosensors and are discussed together with selected application examples to illustrate how engineered coiled-coil interactions support sensitive and specific molecular recognition as well as switchable control in synthetic biology and chemical biology. Overall, this review highlights coiled coils as programmable, stable, and highly designable scaffolds at the interface of molecular engineering, computation, and chemical biology.

title: When does a funnel become a trap? A Gomboc-inspired model of protein folding landscapes.
authors: Shityakov, Sergey; Skorb, Ekaterina V; Nosonovsky, Michael
abstract: The protein folding problem remains a fundamental challenge in biophysics. While energy landscape theory resolves Levinthal's paradox through funnel-shaped landscapes, the quantitative effects of landscape ruggedness on folding kinetics are not fully understood. We introduce a computational model inspired by Gomboc, a convex 3D shape with one stable equilibrium and one unstable equilibrium, as an analogy for protein folding landscapes. Using a tunable ruggedness parameter, we simulate "folding" across multiple ruggedness conditions (r = 0 and r = 10(-8) to 10(-3)), spanning five orders of magnitude in the positive-r regime. At minimal ruggedness (10(-8)), the model achieves 83% success in reaching native-like states. Increasing the ruggedness to 10(-7)-10(-5) reduces the success rate to 25-39%, reflecting landscape trapping as an analog for kinetic trapping in physical folding. Benchmarking against the TPR1 domain via Rosetta and AlphaFold3 reveals native-like coverages of 77% and 90%, respectively, showing qualitative correspondence with the Gomboc model's success rates at low ruggedness. These findings suggest that the Gomboc-inspired model captures essential features of folding landscape quality and may serve as a useful heuristic for comparing foldability across different systems, bridging mathematical topology with protein biophysics.

title: Identification and expression analysis of intergenic long non-coding RNAs (lincRNA) associated with stripe rust resistance in wheat.
authors: Fang, Xiaole; Wang, Xiaoyu; Yang, Tian; Wang, Youning; Ao, Xue; Cao, Peina; Gong, Pan; Ma, Dongfang
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Long intergenic non-coding RNAs (lincRNAs) have emerged as important regulators of plant immune responses, yet their functional landscape in wheat (Triticum aestivum) during stripe rust (Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici) infection remains largely unexplored. METHODS: In this study, a genome-wide identification of lincRNAs was performed using strand-specific RNA-seq data from wheat leaves following Pst inoculation. Functional enrichment, co-expression, lincRNA-miRNA-mRNA network prediction, and AlphaFold-based protein-RNA structure prediction were used to characterize candidate lincRNAs. RESULTS: A total of 2,736 expressed lincRNAs were identified, of which 515 were differentially expressed during infection. Functional enrichment of genes located within 100 kb of the differentially expressed lincRNAs revealed significant associations with defense-related pathways, including MAPK signaling and plant-pathogen interaction. Coordinated expression patterns between lincRNAs and adjacent defense-related mRNAs suggested putative cis-regulatory associations. Furthermore, lincRNA-miRNA-mRNA network prediction identified 65 differentially expressed lincRNAs as potential endogenous target mimics for 21 conserved miRNAs, revealing a widespread competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) regulatory network. Importantly, AlphaFold-based protein-RNA structure prediction demonstrated that the co-expressed lincRNA MSTRG.56980 forms a stable complex with the RGA1-type resistance protein TraesCS6B03G0179100. DISCUSSION: This provides a first computational prediction of a possible physical interaction between a wheat lincRNA and an immune receptor. These integrative findings substantially expand the current understanding of non-coding regulatory networks in wheat immunity and provide a foundational resource for prioritizing candidate lincRNAs as targets for enhancing stripe rust resistance.

title: Machine Learning-Guided Discovery of Novel Inhibitors of Escherichia coli MurB.
authors: Song, Shuhua; Liu, Qingxin; Luo, Aoqi; Shi, Xiao; Si, Xinxin
abstract: MurB, a key enzyme involved in bacterial cell wall biosynthesis, represents a promising target for antibacterial drug discovery. In this study, a machine learning assay was employed to identify potential inhibitors targeting E. coli MurB. Five machine learning models were constructed using AutoMolDesigner, of which the RDKit_2D-based Model_2 was selected as the optimal activity-prediction model for virtual screening of an in-house compound library, yielding 238 compounds. These compounds were subsequently subjected to FRED molecular docking, and 16 candidate compounds were selected based on their hydrogen-bond interactions with the key active-site residue ASN A:233. Preliminary enzyme inhibition assays conducted at 50 muM identified 4 compounds (Q9, Q11, Q12, and Q13) with inhibition rates exceeding 50%. Further IC(5)(0) determination revealed values of 34.44, 31.45, 25.08, and 25.94 muM, respectively. Molecular dynamics simulations combined with principal component analysis were performed to investigate the dynamic behaviors and binding stability of the MurB-ligand complexes. In addition, a CCK-8 assay was conducted in HepG2 cells to evaluate the cytotoxicity of the active compounds preliminarily. Collectively, 4 low-cytotoxic micromolar MurB inhibitors were identified in this study, offering promising scaffolds for further mechanistic investigation and structural optimization.

title: Identification of highly specific bacterial L-asparaginase through genome-wide computational screening and experimental validation.
authors: Janicki, Maciej; Zielezinski, Andrzej; Pierog, Izabela; Sliwiak, Joanna; Ludwikow, Agnieszka; Karlowski, Wojciech M; Jaskolski, Mariusz; Loch, Joanna I
abstract: BACKGROUND: Bacterial L-asparaginases are key therapeutics for acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), but their clinical efficacy is limited by off-target L-glutaminase co-activity, which contributes to severe side effects. This study aimed to identify highly specific bacterial L-asparaginases with minimal L-glutaminase co-activity. METHODS: We screened ~ 85,000 prokaryotic genomes using a workflow integrating AlphaFold2 structure prediction, molecular docking, binding-energy estimation, and molecular dynamics simulations. Six top-ranked enzymes were selected for experimental validation. RESULTS: RhAII protein from Acidobacteriota sp. showed high specificity toward L-asparagine (L-Asn), with a Michaelis constant (K(M)) of 12 +/- 2 microM and turnover number (k(cat)) of 34 +/- 2 s(-)(1), and negligible L-glutaminase activity. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations revealed a relationship between enzyme activity and the conformational dynamics of the flexible gating element (FGE), characterized by residue-level root mean square fluctuation (RMSF), and L-Asn positional fluctuations, evaluated by ligand root mean square deviation (RMSD) relative to the protein. High L-asparaginase activity was associated with optimal FGE dynamics and low L-Asn RMSD, consistent with stable substrate positioning within the active site. In contrast, enzymes with altered FGE dynamics relative to the reference EcAII enzyme from Escherichia coli, such as PoAII from Planctomycetota sp., showed poor L-asparaginase performance (K(M) 5797 +/- 1143 microM; k(cat) 1.2 +/- 0.1 s(-)(1)). CONCLUSIONS: Genome- and structure-guided screening identified RhAII as a promising antileukemic candidate for further validation in biological models. A key limitation of the computational workflow was the lack of correlation between predicted substrate binding energies and catalytic efficiency, highlighting the importance of active-site dynamics in enzyme kinetics.

title: An open structure-guided RNA foundation model for generalizable prediction.
authors: Zhu, Heqin; Li, Ruifeng; Chang, Ao; Chen, Haobin; Zhang, Feng; Tang, Fenghe; Ye, Tong; Li, Xin; Gu, Yunjie; Xiong, Peng; Zhou, S Kevin
abstract: RNA language models have achieved strong performance across diverse downstream tasks by leveraging large-scale sequence data. However, RNA function is fundamentally shaped by hierarchical structure, making structural information important for pre-training. Existing approaches often depend on noisy annotations or task-specific objectives that can limit generalizability. Here we present structRFM, a structure-guided RNA foundation model trained on 21 million RNA sequence-structure pairs by integrating base-pairing interactions into masked language modelling through a pair-matching operation. We also introduce MUSES, a multi-source ensemble of secondary structures designed to mitigate predictor bias, and a dynamic masking ratio that balances structure-guided and nucleotide-level masking. structRFM learns joint sequence and structure representations as sequence-level, nucleotide-level and pairwise features for broad downstream adaptation. It ranks highly in zero-shot homology classification and establishes new benchmarks for secondary-structure prediction. Its tertiary-structure adaptation, Zfold, consistently improves both three-dimensional predictions and their extracted secondary structures, with performance comparable to AlphaFold3(1) across CASP15-natural, CASP16 and RNA-Puzzles. structRFM also improves performance on function-prediction tasks and generalizes to newly released RNA families and long non-coding RNAs. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of structure-guided pre-training and highlight multimodal RNA language models for robust structural and functional inference. The complete 21-million-pair dataset, model weights and source code are openly available to support multimodal RNA foundation-model development.

title: RobPicker: a meta-learning framework for robust identification of macromolecules in cryo-electron tomograms.
authors: Liang, Youwei; Hosseini, Ramtin; Rahmani, Hamidreza; Singh, Digvijay; Zhang, Ruiyi; Zhang, Li; Guo, Han; Choe, Sang; Lee, Joan; Xu, Min; Segal, Eran; Zou, James; Williamson, James; Villa, Elizabeth; Grotjahn, Danielle A; Xie, Pengtao
abstract: Accurate particle picking of macromolecules of diverse types, shapes and sizes in cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) is critical for understanding the molecular architecture of biological systems in their native state. Current deep learning methods have shown potential for identifying macromolecules in tomograms; however, they are vulnerable to annotation noise in the training data and to imbalanced distributions of macromolecule species. Here, to address these limitations, we developed RobPicker, a meta-learning framework that effectively mitigates these issues by automatically learning to correct label errors and by placing greater emphasis on smaller and rarer macromolecule species. In evaluations across diverse cryo-ET datasets with noisy labels and imbalanced species distributions, RobPicker substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly in identifying small and rare macromolecules. The robustness and efficiency of RobPicker led to improved resolution in 3D density maps of protein structures, enabling high-resolution cellular structural biology analysis.

title: Spatial control of karyopherin binding avidity within NPC mimics revealed by designer FG-nucleoporins.
authors: de Vries, Hendrik W; Barth, Anders; Fragasso, Alessio; Otto, Tegan A; van den Berg, Ashmiani; van der Sluis, Eli O; van der Giessen, Erik; Veenhoff, Liesbeth M; Dekker, Cees; Onck, Patrick R
abstract: Nucleocytoplasmic transport occurs via nuclear pore complexes (NPCs), ~40-60 nm wide pores lined with intrinsically disordered proteins that are rich in Phe-Gly motifs (FG-Nups) that form a selective barrier. Molecules larger than ~50 kDa are increasingly blocked for transport unless they are bound to a nuclear transport receptor such as the karyopherin (Kap) family of proteins. How the amino acid sequence of FG-Nups contributes to this selectivity is not fully understood. Here, we present de novo designed artificial FG-Nups with a systematically varied FG-repeat spacing and charge-to-hydrophobicity ratio (C/H). Starting from a reference sequence termed NupY (with the average properties of yeast GLFG-Nups), we design, synthesize, and experimentally test a library of NupY variants using quartz crystal microbalance with dissipation monitoring and phase separation assays. We find that the spacing between FG-motifs governs Kap95 absorption into the FG-Nup phase, while increasing C/H results in higher avidity for Kap95 due to an increased accessibility of FG-motifs. Molecular dynamics simulations of transport through NupY-coated pores show a reduced barrier function for noncohesive variants and the highest transport selectivity for designs close to native GLFG-Nups. We postulate that a balance between steric hindrance and enthalpic gain from multivalent Kap-FG-Nup interactions drives the spatial and temporal partitioning of Kaps in the NPC.

title: Structural basis of phospholipid sensing nuclear receptor LRH-1 recognition by carboxylic acid bioisosteres reveals an alternative ligand interaction site.
authors: Bhowmik, Debipreeta; Cato, Michael L; Abraham, Sarah M; Spurlin, Racheal M; Flynn, Autumn R; Colucci, Jennifer K; Mays, Suzanne; D'Agostino, Emma H; Johnson, Alyssa M; Jui, Nathan T; Calvert, John; Ortlund, Eric A
abstract: Liver receptor homolog-1 (LRH-1; NR5A2) is a phospholipid-sensing nuclear receptor that regulates metabolic and steroidogenic pathways in the liver, intestine, and pancreas. Previously, we showed that small-molecule LRH-1 agonists with carboxylic acid "tails" mimic endogenous phospholipid contacts at the mouth of the ligand-binding pocket, enhancing receptor activation. To improve metabolic stability while preserving these key interactions, we designed a series of agonists in which the carboxylate was replaced with bioisosteric polar groups. Substituting a tetrazole for the carboxylate in a lead agonist preserved high affinity LRH-1 binding, improved potency in cellular reporter assays, and promoted stronger target gene induction. Incorporation of a sulfamide moiety to promote interactions in the deep part of the LRH-1 binding pocket yielded a dual-modified agonist (6NTet) with further gains in affinity and activity. Crystal structures, molecular dynamics simulations, and mutational analyses revealed that the 6NTet tetrazole tail dynamically samples two distinct interaction sites within the LRH-1 ligand-binding pocket. One site corresponds to a previously characterized region engaged by phospholipid ligands and synthetic carboxylate-containing agonists (site 1), whereas the second represents a previously unrecognized interaction site (site 2). Mutational analyses demonstrated that both sites contribute to agonist-induced receptor activation, while site 2 additionally influences basal LRH-1 activity. Together, these findings establish tetrazole substitution as an effective strategy for improving phospholipid-mimetic LRH-1 agonists and identify 6NTet as a promising lead compound. The discovery of a novel ligand interaction site further expands our understanding of LRH-1 activation and provides a framework for next-generation agonist design.

title: Cancer-associated histone tail mutations reshape conformational ensembles and DNA-contact states in nucleosomes.
authors: Wang, Liujin; Zhang, Houfang; Yuan, Xupeng; Mai, Meiru; Zhao, Yunjie; Peng, Yunhui
abstract: Cancer-associated histone mutations can perturb chromatin regulation, yet how many noncanonical mutations in intrinsically disordered histone tails alter nucleosome dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we combine pan-cancer histone mutation profiling with 31.5 mus of all-atom molecular dynamics simulations of complete nucleosomes to investigate recurrent mutations in the H2A, H2B, H3, and H4 tails. We identify recurrent and understudied mutation sites beyond canonical H3 oncohistones and characterize how selected substitutions perturb histone-tail conformational ensembles and DNA contacts in their nucleosomal context. The simulations reveal mutation-specific redistribution of tail-DNA contacts across the nucleosomal DNA surface, accompanied by changes in MM/GBSA-derived relative interaction-energy estimates. For selected systems, Markov state modeling further resolves metastable tail-DNA contact states and shows that mutations alter their structural characteristics and population distributions. These perturbations are not confined to the substituted residues but extend to neighboring interaction networks. Together, our results provide a molecular-level physical picture of how cancer-associated histone-tail mutations reshape conformational and interaction-state landscapes in nucleosomes.

title: Evolutionary Intelligence: How Coevolution Opened the Way to the AlphaFold Revolution.
authors: Bastolla, Ugo; Aurell, Erik; Cocco, Simona; Liberles, David A; Micheletti, Cristian; Orellana, Laura; Rojas, Ana; Talavera, David; Valencia, Alfonso
abstract: The sequences and structures of proteins that exist in nature are a joint product of physical mechanisms and evolutionary processes that are deeply interconnected. It was proposed that physical interactions between amino acids at different protein sites induce evolutionary correlations (co-evolution) between these sites. The inference of these correlations, first as mutual information, then as parameters of a statistical model that describes protein families (direct couplings) and, finally, through the deep neural networks of AlphaFold, produced very powerful developments that revolutionized the field of protein structure and function prediction, providing unprecedented advances in the understanding of proteins and even cells. To discuss the evolutionary mechanisms that produce the correlations exploited by AlphaFold, some of us organized the symposium "Evolutionary intelligence: How coevolution opened the way to the AlphaFold revolution" (Madrid, August 2025), sponsored by the Journal of Molecular Evolution and by the Computational Biology and Bioinformatics (BCB) Hub of the Spanish Research Council (CSIC). The symposium gathered a collection of researchers who contributed to the development and the advancement of the approach based on evolution-induced correlations. This paper represents a collective discussion of part of this community.

title: Targeted Discovery of a Novel Carrageenan-Binding Module with High Affinity through Computational Screening.
authors: Du, Jiawei; Sun, Menghui; Chen, Fangyi; Zheng, Long; Gong, Hongfang; Chang, Yaoguang; Xue, Changhu
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
abstract: Carrageenan is a sulfated red algal polysaccharide widely used in food for its gelling and thickening properties. High-affinity recognition tools are needed for food quality control, and carbohydrate-binding modules (CBMs) are promising recognition elements. However, high-affinity carrageenan-specific CBMs remain scarce. Here, we developed a computationally driven screening strategy integrating structure prediction and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations for targeted high-affinity CBM discovery through binding free energy calculations prior to experimental validation. Using this strategy, a novel CBM designated AmCBM116 was identified from iota-carrageenases of the GH82 family. AmCBM116 specifically recognizes both kappa- and iota-carrageenan with high affinity, with association constants (Ka) of 1.97 x 105 M-1 and 1.82 x 106 M-1, respectively. Key residues involved in ligand recognition were identified. AmCBM116 and its homologues reveal a novel CBM family, CBM116. This study expands the carrageenan-binding CBMs and provides a framework for the targeted discovery of high-affinity polysaccharide-binding modules.

title: Structure-Guided Remodeling of Multi-Substrate Binding Pocket in Nicotinamide Mononucleotide Adenylyltransferase for Efficient NAD+ Synthesis.
authors: Wei, Dianju; Li, Liangjun; Cui, Yuzhi; Huang, Yinfeng; Zou, Shuping; Xue, Yaping; Zheng, Yuguo
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
abstract: The rational engineering of enzymes that coordinate multiple substrates within a confined active site remains a major challenge in biocatalysis. Here, we present a structure-guided dual-cluster engineering strategy that exploits low epistatic coupling among conserved residues to independently tune electronic and geometric active-site features while avoiding trade-offs. This approach was validated through re-engineering Methanothermobacter thermautotrophicus nicotinamide mononucleotide adenylyltransferase. The optimal triple mutant MT3 (V6C/Q10E/P11T) showed a 5.1-fold increase in catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km) over wild type. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed that the mutations synergistically compact the substrate-binding pocket, reduce the catalytic distance by 1.4 A, and reshape local electrostatics to stabilize a near-attack conformation, thereby lowering the reaction barrier. In a 30-L bioreactor, MT3 achieved 85.3% conversion and a titer of 112.5 g L-1 NAD+ within 8 h, underscoring its industrial potential. Collectively, this study provides a transferable framework for engineering complex multisubstrate enzymes by integrating structural dynamics with process-scale validation.

title: The C-terminal Omega-Loop of Candida antarctica Lipase A Governs Active Pocket Exposure via Conformational Switching.
authors: Che, Yanli; Zhang, Jinrui; Li, Mingzhu; Shen, Qi; Li, Jingyan; Lu, Xin; Chen, Yujie
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
abstract: Candida antarctica lipase A (CALA) is widely used in industrial catalysis due to its excellent thermostability and unique substrate selectivity. However, the molecular mechanism governing its active pocket exposure remains unclear, which hampers its further application. In this study, by integrating multiscale simulations and protein engineering, the C-terminal Omega-loop (Loop 3) was identified as the key structural element governing active pocket opening. Truncation or enhancement of flexibility of this loop was found to promote conformational transitions toward the open state. Enzymatic assays revealed that Loop 3 variants shift the optimal substrate from C16 to C14 without altering regioselectivity. Notably, immobilization on hydrophobic supports likely restricts Loop 3 conformation, leading to complete inactivation in anhydrous systems. These results identified Loop 3 as a critical regulator of CALA conformational dynamics, providing a structural basis for rational engineering and immobilization strategy optimization.

title: Structural Rigidity and Nucleophilic Proximity Synergistically Enable Efficient High-Temperature Hydrolysis of Phthalate Esters by PestE.
authors: Chen, Yebao; Rao, Jingwen; Liang, Wenli; Yang, Liu; Hu, Xiaoyan; Dong, Xiaoyu; Wang, Yonghua; Hu, Rongkang
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
abstract: Phthalic acid esters (PAEs) are persistent environmental pollutants. Their industrial biodegradation demands thermostable, efficient hydrolases. We characterized PestE, a thermostable esterase hydrolyzing both dialkyl and monoalkyl PAEs. PestE retained >98% of its maximal activity in short-term assays at 80-100  degrees C, with minimal loss after 12 h, and retained  approximately 50% activity after 48 h at 80  degrees C, with 99.4% dibutyl phthalate degradation in 2 min. Molecular dynamics simulations indicated that hydrophobic core reorganization and increased surface hydrophilicity synergistically enhance thermostability by balancing global rigidity and local flexibility. Co-crystallization with monobutyl phthalate revealed a substrate-guiding tunnel and catalytic machinery (Ser157-His284-Asp254 triad and oxyanion hole Gly85/Gly86/Ala158) for two-step dealkylation. A key feature is the close proximity of the nucleophilic Ser157 to the substrate carbonyl carbon (2.8-3.1 A), enabling efficient catalysis. Mutagenesis confirmed key hydrophobic residues for substrate binding and active-site stability. These findings establish PestE as a promising biocatalyst for industrial PAE degradation.

title: Rosmarinic Acid Inhibits beta-Sheet and beta-Hairpin Formation in Human Islet Amyloid Polypeptide Dimers by Stabilizing Localized C-Terminal Motifs: An REMD Study.
authors: Wang, Gang; Zhu, Xinyi; Zhao, Ziqian; Wu, Xiaoxiao; Qian, Zhenyu
abstract: The misfolding of human islet amyloid polypeptide (hIAPP) into soluble oligomers is a primary pathological event in type 2 diabetes, with the early dimerization process representing a critical pharmacological target. Here, we investigate the molecular mechanism by which rosmarinic acid (RA) counteracts full-length hIAPP self-association through replica-exchange molecular dynamics. Our results show that RA drastically suppresses overall beta-sheet propensities and truncates extended, aggregation-competent beta-strands, lowering the sampled population of ordered beta-hairpin-like motifs associated with amyloidogenic hIAPP conformations. Instead of forming compact structures, the hIAPP dimer is diverted toward disordered, hyper-solvated topologies. This conformational remodeling is driven by spatially heterogeneous thermodynamic perturbations that disrupt native interpeptide contacts and transfer structured motifs into localized turn and bend structures at the C-terminus. Energetically, RA outcompetes peptide-peptide interactions via a multimodal strategy, preferentially anchoring to the hIAPP N-terminus through residues K1 and R11 while simultaneously engaging the hydrophobic core via pi-pi stacking. Notably, this robust noncovalent occupation of key amyloidogenic regions occurs spontaneously in the simulations, offering an atomistic clue for modulating early hIAPP self-association. These structural and energetic insights clarify how RA interacts with transient hIAPP dimer ensembles, providing a defined biophysical framework for the rational design of amyloid inhibitors.

title: Beyond Traditional Use: Mechanistic Insights into the Medicinal Potential of Thymus tiflisiensis and Modulatory Enhancement Effects of Gallic Acid.
authors: Mittova, Valentina; Botchkova, Ekaterina; Tsetskhladze, Zurab R; Eradze, Nino; Motsonelidze, Catherine; Pirtskhalava, Marina; Roviello, Giovanni N
abstract: BACKGROUND: Thymus tiflisiensis is used in Georgian traditional medicine, but its pharmacological properties remain poorly characterized. This study evaluated the antioxidant, protein denaturation inhibitory, and antibacterial activities of leaf and root extracts and examined the modulatory effects of gallic acid (GA) on these activities. METHODS: Methanolic extracts of leaves and roots were analyzed for total phenolic and flavonoid contents, rosmarinic acid (RA), ascorbic acid, and glutathione. Antioxidant activity was evaluated using the DPPH assay, protein denaturation inhibitory activity using a bovine serum albumin denaturation assay, and antibacterial activity against Streptococcus agalactiae and Escherichia coli using broth microdilution. The combined effects of the plant extracts and GA were evaluated across multiple concentration matrices. Molecular docking was used to predict the interactions of RA and GA with the bacterial enzymes MurF and LpxC. RESULTS: The methanolic leaf extract exhibited greater antioxidant activity (IC(50) = 34.8 microg/mL) than the root extract (IC(50) = 81.9 microg/mL), accompanied by higher total phenolic (113.6 vs. 56.9 mg GAE/g DW) and flavonoid (63.8 vs. 19.0 mg RE/g DW) contents and higher ASC/DHA and GSH/GSSG ratios. Conversely, the root extract exhibited greater protein denaturation inhibitory activity (IC(50) = 51.3 vs. 159.7 microg/mL for the leaf extract) and moderate antibacterial activity against S. agalactiae (MIC = 6.0 mg/mL) and contained higher levels of RA. The addition of 5 microM GA enhanced the antioxidant activity of both leaf and root extracts. In protein denaturation assays, 10 microM GA produced a minor enhancement at low extract concentrations, whereas 100 microM GA reduced the inhibitory effects. At 1 mM, GA enhanced the antibacterial activity of both extracts against S. agalactiae and that of the root extract against E. coli. Molecular docking predicted more favorable interactions of RA with MurF and LpxC than those of GA. CONCLUSIONS: T. tiflisiensis root extracts exhibited greater protein denaturation inhibitory and antibacterial activities, whereas leaf extracts showed greater antioxidant activity. GA modulated these activities in a concentration- and tissue-dependent manner, with enhancement observed at specific concentrations and attenuation at higher concentrations in the protein denaturation assay. Exploratory molecular docking predicted favorable interactions of RA with the bacterial enzymes MurF and LpxC. These findings support further investigation of the bioactive properties of T. tiflisiensis and the mechanisms underlying their modulation by GA.

title: AmyloDeep: protein language model-based ensemble model for predicting amyloid propensity from the amino acid sequence.
authors: Davtyan, Alisa; Khachatryan, Anahit; Petrosyan, Rafayel
abstract: MOTIVATION: Amyloids are predominantly beta-sheet-rich, stable protein structures that can maintain their presence in the human body for multiple years. Amyloid protein aggregates contribute to the development of multiple neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and Huntington's, and are involved in different vital functions, such as memory formation and immune system function. RESULTS: Here, we used advanced machine learning and deep learning techniques to predict amyloid propensity from the amino acid sequence. First, we aggregated labeled amino acid sequence data from multiple sources, obtaining a roughly balanced dataset of 2365 sequences for binary classification. We leveraged that data to both fine-tune the ESM2 model and to train new models based on protein embeddings from ESM2 and UniRep. The predictions from these models were then unified into a single soft voting ensemble model, yielding highly robust and accurate results. We further made a tool where users can provide the amino acid sequence and get the amyloid formation probabilities of different segments of the input sequence. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: Users can access the light version of AmyloDeep through the web server at https://amylodeep.com/, and the full model is available as a Python package at https://pypi.org/project/amylodeep/.

title: Bone morphogenetic protein 4 meets artificial intelligence: a comprehensive review of AI-driven advances in drug discovery, structural modeling, and clinical translation.
authors: Sun, Wanli; Huo, Tongtong; Ye, Zhewei; Wei, Wu; Sun, Yanqing; Cai, Hui
abstract: BACKGROUND: Bone Morphogenetic Protein 4 (BMP4), a member of the transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta) superfamily, plays pivotal roles in embryonic development, tissue homeostasis, and disease pathogenesis-including cancer, fibrosis, and fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP). The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methodologies over the past 5 years has created unprecedented opportunities for understanding and therapeutically targeting BMP4 biology at multiple scales, from atomic-resolution structure prediction to population-level clinical prognostication. OBJECTIVE: This review systematically examines the intersection of BMP4 biology and AI across three core domains: (1) AI-driven drug discovery targeting BMP4 signaling pathways, (2) deep learning-based protein structure prediction and computational modeling of BMP4 and its receptor complexes, and (3) clinical AI applications for BMP4-associated diseases. METHODS: A narrative review with systematic search elements was conducted across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, bioRxiv, and arXiv for English-language publications from 2020 to 2026, supplemented by targeted searches via Semantic Scholar. Included studies were categorized as BMP4-specific, BMP receptor/BMP-pathway-targeted, or transferable AI methodology not yet applied to BMP4. RESULTS: We find that AI has accelerated BMP4-related research along multiple axes, though with important caveats. AlphaFold3 and related tools have generated high-confidence predicted models of BMP4-receptor complex architecture, aspects of which were previously intractable to experimental structure determination; these predictions remain to be fully validated experimentally. ML-guided virtual screening has identified first-in-class BMP pathway (receptor) modulators for FOP, although BMP4-specific small-molecule modulators have not yet been identified computationally.
