Single-cell transcriptomics combined with machine learning have revealed BMP4's context-dependent roles in glioblastoma cell state transitions and cancer-associated fibroblast biology; and LASSO-Cox regression models incorporating BMP4 expression have shown promising prognostic value in pancreatic adenocarcinoma and gastric cancer, pending prospective validation. Significant gaps persist-most notably the absence of BMP4-specific de novo protein design efforts, the scarcity of large-scale training datasets for BMP4-targeted drug discovery, and the limited integration of multimodal AI approaches in BMP4 clinical research. CONCLUSION: The convergence of BMP4 biology and AI represents a fertile research Frontier. While foundational tools are now in place, realizing the full translational potential of AI-augmented BMP4 research will require coordinated efforts in data generation, model development, and rigorous experimental and clinical validation. We outline priority directions for the next 5 years (approximately 2026-2031).

title: Conserved proline mutations preserve helical kinks but rewire the activation networks of beta(2)-adrenergic receptor.
authors: Bose, Pritom; Leitner, David M
abstract: Prolines in the transmembrane (TM) region play a pivotal role in the function of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs). In this molecular simulation study, 2 independent sets of trajectories are analyzed for 7 mutations of TM prolines of beta(2)-adrenergic receptor in agonist (Ag)- and inverse-agonist (IAg)-bound states and compared with the wild-type (WT) receptor. A set of structural and contact-based signatures that consistently separate activating from inactivating mutations is identified. While mutation does not substantially alter local protein structure, it leads to numerous structural changes in the protein that affect activity, largely consistent with results of earlier experiments. Comparing the distance between Leu47(2x46) and Leu215(6x37) for Ag- and IAg-bound states with the WT reference, we find activation-like behavior in both trajectories for the 3 mutants experimentally found to be activating-like, and inactivation-like behavior in at least one trajectory for the 4 mutants found experimentally to be inactivating. In addition to the well-recognized TM6 swing, activating-like mutations generate other interhelical rearrangements. Changes involving the TM3-TM6 hydrophobic lock, DRY-TM6 interface, and DRY-NPxxY coupling are important features distinguishing activation-like from inactivation-like responses. A functional shift score is introduced, which helps clarify connections between contact and functional changes due to mutation.

title: Acid-induced conformational remodeling of arachin bidirectionally modulates aflatoxin B1 binding: a multi-spectroscopic and molecular simulation study.
authors: Li, Mohan; Yuan, Jiahao; Zhou, Dian; Chen, Kewei; Du, Muying; Zalan, Zsolt; Awad, Sameh; Kan, Jianquan
abstract: Arachin (Ara), the major storage protein in peanuts, is considered a critical bottleneck limiting the accurate detection and effective detoxification of aflatoxin B1 (AFB1) due to its strong binding affinity for this mycotoxin. However, the structure-activity relationship governing Ara-AFB1 interactions and its response to environmental factors remain poorly understood. In this study, we systematically investigated how acid treatment (pH 3.0 or 5.0) followed by neutralization to pH 8.0 alters the conformation of Ara and consequently affects its binding behavior toward AFB1. Multi-spectroscopy and molecular simulations revealed that pH 5.0 treatment followed by neutralization induced partial unfolding, increased alpha-helix content relative to native Ara, and exposed additional hydrophobic sites, resulting in enhanced AFB1 binding affinity. In contrast, pH 3.0 treatment caused dissociation that was not reversed upon neutralization, accompanied by extensive alpha-helix loss, a marked increase in random coil content, and hydrophobic core disruption, leading to decreased AFB1 binding capacity. Notably, AFB1 may be physically entrapped within acid-induced protein aggregates, which may contribute to the increased difficulty of detection and detoxification. Our findings reveal, for the first time, a bidirectional regulatory mechanism by which pH-driven conformational remodeling of Ara modulates AFB1 binding in opposite directions depending on acid intensity. This work provides mechanistic insights into matrix-associated mycotoxin behavior and offers theoretical support for AFB1 risk management in food processing environments.

title: Folding without glutamine: Proteome-scale removal of a canonical amino acid.
authors: Garciarrubio, Alejandro; Ramos-Cerrillo, Blanca; Morett, Enrique; Segovia, Lorenzo
abstract: All known life uses a canonical alphabet of 20 amino acids, yet which residues are structurally essential remains untested at proteome scale. Isoleucine was recently eliminated from ribosomal proteins in Escherichia coli, establishing that amino acid alphabet reduction is feasible. Here we ask whether an entire amino acid can be eliminated from a proteome, and develop a computational framework to identify the best target. Using two independent approaches - ProteinMPNN structure-based probabilities and multiple sequence alignment conservation - we define "keep-score" as the fraction of positions where the native residue is optimal. Both methods converge on an unexpected candidate: glutamine has the lowest keep-score, with proline and glycine the highest - counter to substitution-matrix intuition. Glutamine's low keep-score is not explained by a single obvious substitute; glutamate is preferred in only 14% of replacements. Removing this target proteome-wide, we replaced every glutamine across 4,148 proteins with ProteinMPNN-optimal alternatives and modeled the resulting sequences with AlphaFold2. The recoded proteome maintained native-like structures: 85.5% of models exceeded a TMscore of 0.8, indistinguishable from the 85.9% baseline for rebuilt native sequences. Orthogonal validation - ESMFold predictions, Rosetta energy calculations, and conformational ensemble comparisons - revealed no evidence of systematic misfolding attributable to glutamine removal. As a consistency check, a glutamine-free TEM-1 beta-lactamase designed with ProteinMPNN conferred ampicillin resistance in E. coli, indicating fold preservation can extend to biological function. Evolutionary evidence further supports these findings: 24% of E. coli proteins have glutamine-free orthologs in prokaryotic genomes, and glutamine ranks lowest in keep-score in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. These results show that an entire amino acid can be removed from a proteome with folds broadly preserved, establishing keep-score as a general framework and glutamine as the primary candidate for recoding. Crucially, this reflects a computational analysis of structural replaceability, not a demonstration of biological dispensability.

title: Cooling fast and slow: Characterizing the effects of vitrification in cryo-EM and the subsequent recovery of equilibrium populations.
authors: Clark, Robert; Smith, Louis G; Leighton, Matthew P; Szukalo, Ryan J; Khalid, Syma; Debenedetti, Pablo G; Cossio, Pilar; Astore, Miro A; Hanson, Sonya M
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
abstract: Single-particle cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM), a powerful class of techniques in structural biology with the potential to resolve molecular ensembles, requires that samples be vitrified to protect them from the high vacuum of the electron microscope. However, the effects of vitrification on biomolecular ensembles are unknown. To study them, we carried out extensive molecular dynamics simulations (over 50 ms) of the Trp-cage miniprotein at equilibrium and undergoing rapid cooling. We simulated seven cooling rates spanning three orders of magnitude, with the slowest coolings matching experimental rates. By inspecting molecular mobility and density-temperature trajectories for water with and without protein, we found that water vitrification is unaltered by the protein. To track protein conformation changes, and to relate them to kinetics, we made a Markov State Model (MSM) of Trp-cage from 5.4 ms of equilibrium sampling at 277 K. We observed that MSM states with a characteristic time longer than the duration of the nonequilibrium cooling tend to be more robust to artifacts induced by such cooling. Critically, although we observe that some states vanish in the equilibrium ensemble at 230 K, none do in our nonequilibrium cooled ensembles. To account for these perturbations, we developed a thermodynamic inference framework for recovering equilibrium populations from vitrified ensembles. These results indicate that cryo-EM has the capacity to be an accurate technique for the study of biomolecular ensembles.

title: A Comparative Biophysical Study of Conserved Ubiquitin-like Protein Folds.
authors: Bhate, Suhas; Fauzdar, Neeraj Kumar; Chatterjee, Kiran Sankar; Kamma, Harika; Arya, Hemant; Bhatt, Tarun Kumar; Das, Ranabir; Singh, Gajendra
abstract: Ubiquitin and ubiquitin-like proteins (Ubls) constitute a conserved protein family that shares a common beta-grasp structural fold despite substantial sequence and functional divergence. How this highly conserved fold is maintained while accommodating diverse biological functions remains an open question in protein structural biology. In this study, we provide atomistic insights into the structural features that determine the stability of these conserved ubiquitin-like folds. Using an integrated biophysical approach combining solution NMR spectroscopy, molecular dynamics simulations, and chemical denaturation experiments, we systematically compare the protein dynamics and thermodynamic stability of ubiquitin and representative Ubls, including SUMO1, SUMO2, NEDD8, and Hub1. Our results reveal that ubiquitin exhibits exceptional thermodynamic stability relative to other Ubls, whereas Ubls display a broad range of stability profiles without a uniform trend toward destabilization. Biophysical and molecular dynamics analyses show that the reduced stability of Ubls is not associated with the loss of the conserved fold but is accompanied by differences in local structural flexibility. Together, these findings indicate that the conserved ubiquitin fold has been maintained despite sequence divergence and variation in stability and dynamics, supporting functional diversity while preserving structural integrity.

title: Beyond the Active Site: Allosteric Tail of HIV-1 Protease Is a Potential Target for Inhibiting Dimerization.
authors: Dakshinamoorthy, Avinash; Senapati, Sanjib
abstract: HIV protease (HIVPR) is one of the key targets in AIDS therapy. All ten FDA-approved drugs targeting this enzyme compete with the substrates in binding to its active site. However, the emergence of drug-resistant mutants in active and nonactive sites of HIVPR has compromised the efficacy of these drugs. Nonetheless, darunavir (DRV) and tipranavir (TPV) have exhibited greater success than the other eight drugs, presumably due to their dual mode of action: (i) inhibiting protease activity and (ii) blocking protease dimerization. Although crystal structures have explained the inhibitory mechanism of protease activity, the mechanism of inhibiting the dimerization process is poorly understood. In this study, we employ advanced molecular dynamics simulation methods to identify the precise binding motifs of DRV and TPV with monomeric HIVPR. Our results suggest that both inhibitors bind stably to an allosteric pocket located in the tail region of the enzyme. Results also elucidate reversible association-dissociation of the drugs between the conventional active site and the newly identified tail cavity through surface diffusion. Structural analysis revealed that drug binding to the tail pocket induces a conformational extension of the C-terminal alpha-helix, a change that sequesters the terminal residues required for stable dimer formation. Our finding aligns very well with the reported ESI-MS spectra showing the tail interface as a crucial domain in forming a stable HIV protease dimer. Our result paves the way for designing a new class of HIVPR drugs that could target the C-terminal to effectively lock it in the monomeric form, potentially bypassing the cross-resistance due to active-site mutations.

title: EvoSeq-ML: Advancing Data-Centric Machine Learning with Evolutionary-Informed Protein Sequence Representation and Generation.
authors: Mardikoraem, Mehrsa; Pascual, Nathaniel; Eaves, Joelle N; Chatterjee, Shramana; Garland, Logan; VanAntwerp, James; Mahama, Anton; Finneran, Patrick; Hausinger, Robert P; Woldring, Daniel R
abstract: From protein structure prediction to novel protein generation, challenging protein engineering tasks have been made possible by advancements in machine learning (ML). While largely driven by ML architecture refinements, these advancements in ML-based protein engineering campaigns have left the impact of data curation underexplored. In light of the growing wealth of labeled sequence data, data-centric advances (e.g. prioritizing improvements in ML protein engineering tools through the curation of high-quality, domain-specific training data) are increasingly preferred over model-centric advancements. Implementing datasets that accurately reflect biological complexity and diversity has been shown to improve the efficiency of training protein engineering ML tools. Here, we evaluate an ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR)-informed data augmentation strategy for training generative and representation-learning models in protein engineering. Using ethylene-forming enzyme (EFE) as a model system, we show that variational autoencoder models trained on ancestral and near-ancestral sequence datasets generate variants with improved predicted and experimentally measured thermostability relative to variants generated from modern-sequence training data. All experimentally tested ancestral and ML-generated EFEs produced detectable ethylene, although ML-generated variants showed reduced activity relative to wild-type EFE, indicating that the approach more strongly captured stability-associated features than catalytic optimization. We further evaluated ASR-enriched sequence sets for fine-tuning ESM2 representations in endolysin and lysozyme C stability-classification tasks, where ancestral representations were competitive with modern-sequence fine-tuning in selected settings. Overall, this work supports ASR-informed data augmentation as a promising strategy for stability-oriented protein sequence generation and motivates future work to couple ancestral sequence diversity with explicit functional selection.

title: LM2KM: feature extraction from pretrained protein and molecular language models combined with quantum mechanics (QM) features for K (M) predictions.
authors: Zhai, Jingchen; Cai, Lianjin; Niu, Taoyu; Xie, Lei; Wang, Junmei
abstract: The Michaelis constant (K (M)) is a key parameter for characterizing enzyme-substrate interactions and plays an essential role in enzyme kinetics modeling and physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) applications. However, experimental determination of K (M) is labor-intensive, and existing computational prediction approaches remain limited in accuracy and scalability. In this study, we systematically evaluated pretrained protein and molecule language models for K (M) prediction by integrating four protein language models (PLMs) and two molecule language models (MLMs) to encode enzyme sequences and substrate structures, respectively. Principal component analysis (PCA) was applied to reduce feature dimensionality, and a wide range of representation combinations were assessed. Our results indicated that protein representations derived from the last four layers of ProtT5 using approximately 70 features, combined with 20 CLS-based molecular features from MolFormer, provided a well-balanced and efficient representation for K (M) prediction. In addition, the incorporation of quantum mechanics (QM) descriptors consistently improved prediction performance across all tested configurations, with the model R (2) of 0.537. In summary, this work provides a flexible and extensible framework for large-scale K (M) prediction, with strong potential to facilitate enzyme pathway identification, drug and lead screening, and sequence-based protein design, supporting broader applications in enzyme kinetics-driven modeling and drug development.

title: From structure prediction to ligand-target recognition: expanding the reach of AlphaFold in natural product research.
authors: Xu, Guangrui; Hu, Haifeng; Zhao, Weihui; Liu, Zhengxi; Wang, Ting; Liu, Rui; Liu, Song
abstract: Natural products constitute a structurally diverse reservoir of bioactive molecules and remain an important source of lead compounds for drug discovery. However, the limited availability of structural information on pharmacological targets and biomolecular interactions continues to hinder mechanism elucidation and structure-guided optimization, particularly for complex natural products such as bioactive peptides, proteinaceous natural products, and natural molecular glues. Recent advances in AlphaFold have transformed structural biology by enabling high-confidence prediction of protein structures and biomolecular complexes, providing unprecedented opportunities for structure-guided natural product research. Beyond conventional structure-based virtual screening, emerging co-folding strategies have demonstrated considerable potential for improving early enrichment in natural product screening and for elucidating the binding mechanisms of complex natural products with their targets. This review summarizes recent advances in AlphaFold-assisted natural product research, including target structure prediction, hit and lead discovery, co-folding-enabled interaction analysis, mechanistic investigation of peptide- and protein-derived natural products, and the emerging potential of AlphaFold for natural molecular glue discovery. We further discuss current limitations and future directions in structure prediction and interaction modeling. Overall, AlphaFold is reshaping natural product research from lead discovery to mechanistic characterization, with particular promise for advancing macromolecular natural products and molecular glue-mediated therapeutics.

title: InterPro: the protein sequence classification resource in 2027.
authors: Blum, Matthias; Andreeva, Antonina; Chuguransky, Sara; Florentino, Laise Cavalcanti; Flores, Nicole Morveli; Grego, Tiago; Hobbs, Emma Elizabeth Mary; Pinto, Beatriz Lazaro; Polignano, Alessandro; Meng-Papaxanthos, Laetitia; Llinares-Lopez, Felipe; Colwell, Lucy; Marchler-Bauer, Aron; Bordin, Nicola; Bridge, Alan; Haft, Daniel H; Klimke, William; Letunic, Ivica; Mi, Huaiyu; Natale, Darren A; Orengo, Christine A; Piovesan, Damiano; Rivoire, Catherine; Sigrist, Christian J A; Thomas, Paul D; Tosatto, Silvio C E; Wu, Cathy H; Bateman, Alex
abstract: InterPro (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/interpro) is a freely accessible resource for the classification of protein sequences. It integrates predictive models, known as signatures, from multiple member databases to classify sequences into families and to predict the presence of domains and functionally important sites. The InterPro database provides annotations for hundreds of millions of sequences, ensuring extensive coverage of UniProtKB, the standard repository of protein sequences, and includes mapping to several other major resources, such as Gene Ontology, the Protein Data Bank in Europe (PDBe), and the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database. In this publication we report on the status of InterPro (version 110.0), detailing new developments in the database, its associated web interface, and software. Notable updates include InterPro-N, a deep-learning method that increases sequence coverage of UniProtKB to over 90%; the transition from InterProScan 5 to the completely re-engineered InterProScan 6; the integration of structure-based domain classifications and predicted structures from AlphaFold; a redesigned protein viewer offering a concise summary view; and a new Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that allows AI assistants to query InterPro programmatically. Over the past two years, 9484 new InterPro entries have been created, bringing the total to 54 922. InterPro data, software and tools are freely available.

title: Crystallographic fragment screening in cancer and antiviral drug discovery: from electron density to translational outcomes.
authors: Balikci, Esra; Grimes, Jonathan M
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Crystallographic fragment screening (CFS) provides an experimental starting point for small-molecule discovery by defining a fragment's binding site, pose and routes for chemical elaboration. By establishing a structural hypothesis before major medicinal-chemistry investment, CFS reduces early uncertainty and the risk of pursuing a binding mode inferred from activity or modeling but not supported by experimental structural evidence. AREAS COVERED: This review examines how CFS advances fragments into lead series, preclinical candidates and clinical molecules. Oncology examples include kinase inhibitors, the PHIP2 bromodomain, the transcription factor brachyury and the metabolic enzyme PYCR1. Antiviral examples include viral proteases, polymerases, the influenza PA endonuclease and the SARS-CoV-2 immune-evasion protein Mac1. It also considers the practical requirements and limitations of CFS, criteria for hit validation and prioritization, and how high-throughput crystallography, reusable structural datasets and computational or machine-learning methods can support chemical elaboration and translational decision-making. Relevant literature was identified through targeted PubMed searches conducted from March to September 2026, supplemented by reference-list screening of relevant primary studies and reviews. EXPERT OPINION: CFS is most powerful when it provides an experimentally grounded binding hypothesis early in discovery. It converts weak binding into actionable geometry, reveals ligandable pockets and supplies credible design starting points. Computational and machine-learning methods can extend this information by exploring chemical space, ranking fragment elaborations and supporting multiparameter prioritization, but they do not replace experimental determination of binding modes or functional validation. Future progress will depend on reusable structure-affinity datasets and tighter structure-design-synthesis-test cycles that connect crystallographic evidence to biological decisions.

title: Domain-Aware Enzyme Classification via Multiple Instance Learning.
authors: Xiao, Qingyang; Ye, Yuzhen; Tang, Haixu
abstract: MOTIVATION: Accurate Enzyme Commission (EC) number prediction is fundamental to protein function annotation and metabolic pathway reconstruction. Recent methods based on protein language model embeddings or 3D structure have improved EC prediction, but important limitations remain. Whole-sequence embeddings can dilute local functional signals, such as catalytic residues and functional domains, whereas structure-based methods depend on accurate protein structures and are therefore difficult to apply broadly. RESULTS: We present MIL-BC, a multiple instance learning framework for EC prediction that models each protein as a bag of domains rather than a single sequence-level object. This design is motivated by the observation that enzymatic function is often determined by constituent functional domains instead of the full-length sequence alone. Domain instances are generated automatically using our DCTdomain algorithm, avoiding dependence on curated domain annotations. MIL-BC aggregates domain-level evidence into protein-level EC predictions and assigns interpretable weights to domains that contribute most strongly to each prediction. We further combine the domain embedding with global embedding in MIL-BC+. MIL-BC+ achieved F1 improvements of 0.03 - 0.17 over the sequence-based baseline on all four test sets. The largest gains were observed for proteins with multiple enzymatic functions, where domain-level modeling better separates mixed functional signals. These results show that domain-centric multiple instance learning is an accurate and interpretable strategy for enzyme classification. By improving EC prediction without requiring structural data or curated domain labels, MIL-BC provides a scalable framework for large-scale protein function annotation. AVAILABILITY: Code is available as a GitHub repository at https://github.com/omics-ai/enzyme-mil.git.

title: Substrate coupling and inhibition in human Na(+)-dependent Cl(-)/HCO(3)(-) exchanger NCBE (SLC4A10).
authors: Sun, Peixin; Wang, Xinmin; Huang, Yang; Zhang, Jinlun Kylian; Shen, Xurui; Dong, Anqi; Wang, Shiliang; Guo, Xiaojun; Shi, Guoming; Ding, Jing; Chi, Yudan; Yang, Hanting
abstract: Maintaining pH homoeostasis is essential for neuronal excitability and for regulating cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). The Na(+)-dependent Cl(-)/HCO(3)(-) exchanger, NCBE (SLC4A10), abundant in the choroid plexus, contributes to CSF pH control by mediating bicarbonate flux, yet its molecular mechanism has remained unclear. Here we report cryo-EM structures of human NCBE in multiple functional states, revealing conserved binding sites for Na(+), Cl(-), and HCO(3)(-), as well as an unexpected K(+) site indicating relaxed cation selectivity. The inhibitor DIDS binds above the substrate cavity, locking NCBE in an outward-facing conformation and defining a subfamily-selective inhibitory mechanism. Functional assays and molecular dynamics simulations support the coordination of ions and the inhibitory effects. Comparison with an AlphaFold3-predicted inward-facing model suggests an elevator-like transport mechanism and delineates the conformational transitions in Na(+)-dependent HCO(3)(-) transporters. Together, these findings establish a structural framework for NCBE and offer insights into ion coupling and pharmacological modulation within the SLC4 family.

title: Rational design of hydrophobic deep eutectic solvents tunes the catalytic pocket of lipase for the sustainable synthesis of structural lipids.
authors: Han, Yiran; Chen, Zhiheng; Fang, Hao; Hu, Yi; Nian, Binbin
abstract: The global epidemic of metabolic diseases has accelerated the demand for functional structured lipids, particularly medium- and long-chain triacylglycerols (MLCTs), which have attracted significant attention due to their dual advantages of rapid energy supply and provision of essential fatty acids. However, the enzymatic synthesis of MLCTs has long been constrained by the solvent-enzyme compatibility paradox, wherein solvents capable of effectively dissolving hydrophobic substrates tend to strip the essential water layer from the enzyme, leading to catalytic failure. Here, we report a strategy with notable improvement potential that overcomes this bottleneck by employing a rationally designed hydrophobic deep eutectic solvent (DESs) system, cyclohexanone and lauric acid at a 2:1 ratio. Systematic screening of 44 solvent systems revealed that this specific DESs enables Candida antarctica Lipase B (Novozym 435) to achieve an outstanding yield of 88.17% +/- 1.42% under optimized conditions (55  degrees C, 24 h), significantly outperforming conventional organic solvents. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations further unveiled its unique microscopic mechanism: the hydrophobic DES not only acts as a reaction medium but also actively modulates the enzyme's catalytic pocket. By stabilizing the open conformation of the lipase lid region (alpha5 and alpha10 helices) and maintaining an optimal pocket volume (V(index) = 1.11), this solvent system significantly enhances the substrate binding free energy to -122.25 kJ/mol, thereby promoting proper substrate anchoring. Moreover, the system demonstrates excellent industrial robustness, retaining over 90% of enzyme activity after five reuse cycles. This study establishes an alternative pathway distinct from mainstream frameworks of solvent-guided enzymatic reaction engineering, where rational design of non-biological media is used to regulate the machinery of biological macromolecules, providing a new theoretical foundation for green biomanufacturing.

title: pLM-bVAE: protein language model-enhanced binary representation improves quantum annealing-based protein sequence design
authors: Hiromi H Ueda; Andrejs Tučs; Koji Tsuda; Mitsuo Umetsu; Yutaka Saito
abstract: Quantum annealing (QA) has been explored as an approach for protein design in vast combinatorial sequence spaces. Applying QA to protein sequence design requires amino acid sequences to be encoded as binary vectors, and optimized vectors to be decoded back into amino acid sequences. Thus, both the quality of binary encoding and sequence reconstruction accuracy are important for effective QA-based optimization. Binary variational autoencoder (bVAE) has been used to map protein sequences to binary representations in QA-based protein sequence design. However, bVAE was originally developed for natural language modeling, and its suitability for proteins has not been systematically evaluated. Here, we present pLM-bVAE, which incorporates protein representations derived from a pretrained protein language model (pLM) into the original bVAE model. In computational experiments on three public protein variant datasets, pLM-bVAE showed higher sequence reconstruction accuracy and binary encoding performance than bVAE. Moreover, we incorporated pLM-bVAE into a QA-based protein sequence design framework. Across all three datasets, pLM-bVAE generated more high-scoring sequences with greater sequence dissimilarity from the training and validation data than bVAE. Our results demonstrate that pLM-bVAE provides an effective binary representation for improving QA-based protein sequence design. Availability The source code used in this manuscript is available at https://github.com/hueda8/pLM-bVAE.

title: FoldAbS: Repurposing the Protein Folding Model as a Foundation Encoder for Antibody Screening
authors: Jun Wu; Fandi Wu; Xinyuan Zhu; Dawei Huang; Kaiwen Cheng; Jianzhu Ma; Fuli Feng; Jianhua Yao
abstract: Therapeutic antibody screening requires prioritizing antibody candidates across specificity, affinity, and developability. Current pipelines typically silo these objectives and underuse structural information that governs antibody-antigen recognition. To address these inefficacies, we introduce FoldAbS, a unified supervised screening framework that reconceptualizes protein folding models as frozen foundation encoders, exploiting their internal representations to capture rich sequence, geometric, and interaction dynamics well beyond basic structure prediction. By coupling the folding model with lightweight, task-specific heads, FoldAbS seamlessly evaluates all three therapeutic criteria within a single architecture. Instantiating this framework with the open-source Protenix model (FoldAbS-Px) yields consistent improvements over baseline approaches, achieving significant performance gains of up to 13.1%, 9.2%, and 6.2% in specificity, affinity, and developability, respectively. Collectively, these results reposition protein folding models from structure predictors and confidence scorers into reusable foundation encoders for comprehensive and supervised antibody screening. Our code is available at https://github.com/nohandsomewujun/FoldAbS.

title: A protein language model for domain, functional site, and variant effect prediction
authors: Peng Wang; Mian Umair Ahsan; Tingting Chen; Kai Wang
abstract: Protein sequence databases are growing far faster than experimentally curated annotations, limiting functional interpretation of newly identified proteins and coding variants. We developed PALM, a protein annotation language model that jointly predicts domain and functional-site occurrence, while preserving overlapping and nested annotations through a soft-target objective. PALM integrates ESM2 with low-rank adaptation (LoRA), learned layer aggregation, and a bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) encoder. PALM was trained on ~15 million InterPro-annotated UniRef50 sequences spanning 17,951 domain and 1,383 site classes. Across 2.3 million held-out proteins, PALM achieved domain- and site-occurrence F1 scores of 0.941 and 0.877, respectively, and retained substantial performance in proteins with <20% sequence identity to the training and validation data. PALM also substantially outperformed ESM3 annotation baseline. Without training on variant-pathogenicity labels, PALM embedding disruption distinguished 151,823 ClinVar missense variants more accurately than ESM2 embedding disruption (AUROC 0.835 versus 0.710), and combining PALM embedding disruption with the ESM2 likelihood-ratio signal reached an AUROC of 0.877. The same combined zero-shot score outperformed AlphaMissense on a benchmark dataset on 128,161 missense variants, that were derived from literature but not present in ClinVar database. At the protein level, PALM embeddings showed stronger CATH-Gene3D superfamily organization than frozen ESM2 and ESM3 embeddings, and improved prediction of experimental activation and repression effects when combined with ESM2. In a downstream case study, we demonstrated the ability to use PALM-derived embedding as proxy of deep mutational scanning (DMS), showcasing the broad application of PALM. Together, PALM converts curated residue-level knowledge into transferable and mechanistically interpretable representations that connect protein sequence, function, and variant consequence.

title: Differentiable Spin-Center Diffusion Model Enables DEER-Guided Generative Pipeline of Weighted Protein Ensembles
authors: Te-Yu Kao; Jens Meiler; Hassane S. Mchaourab
abstract: Biological function entails the interconversion of a protein between distinct conformations, an equilibrium modulated by ligands and other physicochemical conditions. Double electron-electron resonance (DEER) spectroscopy captures these ensembles as distance distributions, P(r), between spin label pairs. However, the width of P(r) convolves protein conformational heterogeneity with the rotameric flexibility of the label. Because current spin label models overestimate this contribution, translating P(r) into ensembles has remained indirect and predominantly qualitative. Here, we developed spin-center (SC) diffusion, a differentiable model of the spin label with a tunable spin label rotameric width. Coupled to a frozen Boltz-2 structure generator, SC diffusion enables the entire experimental P(r) to guide ensemble generation at inference time. We demonstrate the robustness of this pipeline on synthetic P(r) of known composition, recovering the ensemble populations, including both components of a bimodal profile. Guided by experimental P(r) measured under different biochemical conditions, ensembles of the transporters PfMATE, LmrP, MhsT and P-glycoprotein were modeled and free energy differences derived from the ensembles in a condition-dependent manner. By embedding a differentiable label model in structure generation, our approach interprets DEER distributions as weighted conformational ensembles, adding a missing thermodynamic grounding to generative protein structure prediction methods.

title: Omics-scale decoding of protein N-glycosylation using protein language model embeddings
authors: Xiao Zhou; Xingyue Guan; Yao Zhou; Jie Wang; Zhiyu Peng; Weitong Ren; Wei Wang; Ran Xie; Wenfei Li
abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) learn rich sequence semantics from vast volume of protein sequences, yet the information encoded in their high-dimensional embeddings remains largely a black box, posing an interpretability challenge. Here we show that semantic features learned by pLMs can be decoded to reveal biologically meaningful signals using coevolutionary analysis without downstream supervised-training. Building on this insight, we developed MaskNGly, a zero-shot framework that identifies protein N‑glycosylation sites directly from PLM-embeddings while achieving performance comparable to state-of-the-art supervised predictors. MaskNGly is computationally efficient and intrinsically transferable, enabling omics-scale characterization of protein glycosylation landscape. Applied across proteomes, it reveals that canonical N-X-S/T motifs gain higher glycosylation propensities with increasing organismal complexity and that glycosylation preferentially occurs at structured, solvent‑exposed regions. Mutations altering high-scoring motifs are more frequently disease-associated. The framework also captures signatures of glycosylation‑mediated protein allostery. These results establish an interpretable and scalable route to study glycobiology from pLM-embeddings.

title: CryoID2: deep learning-enhanced identification of protein and RNA from cryoEM maps
authors: Qibo Xu; Xinye Yu; Leon Wu; Shi Feng; Z. Hong Zhou
abstract: Identifying the molecular components of cryoEM/cryoET maps of endogenous or poorly characterized complexes remains a major bottleneck. CryoID2 addresses this by integrating deep learning–based feature prediction with sequence prioritization and structural evaluation. Three 3D U-Nets extract structure classes, key-atom positions, and reduced residue/nucleotide types from the input map. These predictions support backbone tracing and the generation of short sequence queries that rank candidates from a user-supplied pool—using BLASTp for proteins and a maximin strategy for RNA. Corresponding PDB or AlphaFold models are then retrieved, rigidly fitted using predicted features and experimental density, and ranked by map agreement. Module-level tests show high-recall feature prediction and resolution-dependent atom clustering, while a 52-case benchmark recovers near-reference fitting quality. In practice, cryoID2 correctly identified PfA-M17 from a 166-protein mass-spectrometry pool and the unannotated Ca-raiA RNA from a genome-derived non-coding sequence set, demonstrating a unified sequence-plus-structure route to molecular identification in cryoEM maps.

title: Protify: A Benchmarking Platform Revealing Task Dependence and Homology Leakage in Protein Language Model Evaluation
authors: Nikolaos Rafailidis; Logan P Hallee; Tamar Peleg; Colin Horger; Luck Haviland; Jason P Gleghorn
abstract: Protein Language Models (pLMs) have become essential tools for computational protein analysis, and the rapid proliferation of architectures, training objectives, and pretraining corpora has produced a diverse and expanding model landscape. Evaluation practices, however, remain fragmented: studies use different datasets, preprocessing pipelines, and reporting conventions, so results rarely transfer between publications. Here we introduce Protify, an open-source platform that standardizes pLM benchmarking across zero-shot, supervised, and transferlearning settings through a unified, low-code interface. Protify currently supports 35 pretrained models and 61 curated datasets and it is easy to add custom versions of each. Leveraging Protify's high throughput pipelines, we benchmarked 23 models on ProteinGym, discovering that DPLM3B is currently the top-performing self-supervised encoder. Another large-scale supervised evaluation across 32 diverse tasks, spanning enzyme classification, gene ontology annotation, protein-protein interaction, subcellular localization, and other functional properties, found that no single pLM dominated: 14 different models took the top score on at least one dataset, and the margins between the best and second-best models fell within run-to-run variability. On enzyme optimal pH prediction, a general-purpose probe pipeline matched or exceeded EpHod, a specialized model selected from 11,550 training runs, after 50 hyperparameter trials (R2 = 0.482 versus 0.425). Under a homology-controlled split of the same data, every pooled-embedding probe collapsed to near-zero R2, and only a transformer probe over full residue embeddings recovered appreciable signal (R2 = 0.248). Model rankings therefore depend as much on evaluation design as on the models themselves. Protify makes those design choices explicit, controlled, and replayable, and is freely available at https://github.com/Gleghorn-Lab/Protify.

title: Improving Molecular Docking Pose Recovery through Targeted Side-Chain Monte Carlo Sampling of an Apo Structure
authors: Subramani P; Shekhar M
abstract: Receptor flexibility complicates molecular docking when only an unbound (apo) protein structure is available. Local side-chain rearrangements can alter binding-pocket accessibility and ligand complementarity, motivating approaches that sample these motions efficiently. Here, we evaluate a targeted Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) protocol that combines local and larger side-chain torsional proposals with periodic molecular dynamics (MD) relaxation under harmonic backbone restraints. Receptor ensembles generated from an apo structure were evaluated against 859 experimental complexes from the OpenBind 2A protease benchmark and compared with the apo receptor and ensembles generated by restrained and unrestrained MD. With regular-space representative selection, MCMC recovered a ligand pose within 2 Å of the experimental pose for 74.4% of complexes, compared with 51.0% for apo and 59.5% for restrained MD. Median minimum ligand heavy-atom RMSD decreased from 1.96 Å for apo and 1.82 Å for restrained MD to 1.62 Å for MCMC. The largest gains occurred for complexes with greater side-chain displacement relative to pocket backbone displacement, consistent with the motions targeted by the protocol. MCMC representatives retained pocket geometries within the experimentally observed range, whereas unrestrained-MD representatives exhibited reduced pocket free volume and poor recovery. These findings support targeted side-chain sampling as a practical approach to generating apo-derived docking ensembles. The reported improvements measure best-case pose coverage across generated poses and receptors; their extension to prospective pose ranking and virtual screening remains to be established.

title: Learning inhibitor interactions from protein deep mutational scanning data and deep learning models
authors: Zou Z; Hazelwood I; Estevam G; Rao J; Chrispens K; Howard MK; Coyote-Maestas W; Fraser JS
abstract: Recent advances in protein language models, geometric deep learning, and structure prediction frameworks have the potential to accelerate computational drug discovery. However, it remains unclear how well these methods generalize beyond their training sets. Mutation-dependent drug responses present a challenge to these methods because there are often large effects from relatively small perturbations. Here, we systematically benchmark diverse mutational effect and drug-target affinity prediction models using deep mutational scanning datasets spanning 11 inhibitor conditions for the MET kinase domain. Across both mutational effect prediction and drug–target affinity tasks, current AI models produce largely ligand-invariant predictions despite experimentally distinct inhibitor-dependent fitness landscapes. Ligand-aware geometric models, including LigandMPNN and LASErMPNN, partially recover experimentally validated resistance-associated hotspots, highlighting the importance of explicitly modeling protein–ligand interactions and local structural flexibility. In contrast, deep learning affinity prediction models underestimate mutation-induced changes in binding affinity. This deficiency likely reflects mutation-invariant structural priors derived from co-folded structure prediction frameworks and the absence of mutation-conditioned supervision in current affinity datasets. Finally, we further extended our analysis to several kinase-inhibitor deep mutational scanning datasets and confirm the overall trends. Our findings suggest that a primary limitation in improving performance on this task lies in the scarcity of mutation-conditioned protein-ligand training data rather than model architecture alone.

title: A validation approach for RNA structures based on deep-learning 3D-structure predictions
authors: Voorspoels A; Simpkin AJ; Keegan RM; Chojnowski G; Rigden DJ
abstract: Understanding the molecular mechanisms of life depends on accurate macromolecular structures. RNA, in particular, poses a particular challenge for structural biology due to its inherent flexibility and dynamic nature. The challenging nature of structure determination experiments and their interpretation have led to the development of validation approaches to prevent or fix errors in solved structures. Existing methods for RNA structure validation can, as with proteins, be broadly split into two types. Map-based validation tools seek to detect discrepancies between the experimental data and the determined structure. They are excellent for fixing all types of errors, but only when high-resolution experimental data are available. Model-only validation methods, which usually focus on molecular geometry, are excellent for fixing short-lengthscale issues even when experimental resolution is low. Conkit-validate is a mapless method for protein validation, which is not based on chemical plausibility, but rather on the similarity between experimental models and structure predictions for the same protein. By comparing contact patterns, this tool leverages evolutionary covariance information, learned by state-of-the-art structural prediction models, into a mapless validation method capable of detecting sequence assignment issues, with notable success in detecting register errors. Here, we extend the conkit-validate method to work on RNA. The results show performance similar to that previously achieved for proteins. In a scan of the PDB, its detection rate does not depend on the local resolution of the density, so it remains applicable where map-based approaches are not, and case studies show it can identify register errors where the density alone cannot decide between models. Together, this highlights the complementary value of a contact-prediction based validation approach using information orthogonal to map- and geometry-based approaches to ensure the quality of deposited RNA structures against varying criteria. The performance of the method can be expected to track ongoing improvements in RNA structure prediction methods.

title: LIMBER: A Hybrid RNA Foundation Model for Predicting and Understanding RNA Structure and Function
authors: Wang Z; Qiu Y; He Y; Thompson I; Wang H; Porter A; Li A
abstract: RNA foundation models offer a promising route to decoding the relationships between RNA sequence, structure and function, yet how model shapes the acquisition and organization of biological information remains poorly understood. Here we introduce Layer-Interleaved Mamba-Bidirectional Encoder for RNA (LIMBER), a hybrid foundation model integrating bidirectional self-attention with selective state-space modeling, pre-trained on 40.5 million non-coding RNA sequences. Through task-specific fine-tuning, LIMBER achieves leading performance on secondary-structure prediction and non-coding RNA classification benchmarks, while demonstrating strong transferability to translation-related tasks and RNA–small-molecule interaction prediction. Beyond model development, we establish a unified, task-agnostic framework to systematically evaluate and interpret the biological knowledge intrinsically acquired by RNA foundation models. This framework validates LIMBER’s strong capabilities in recovering RNA structures and predicting mutational effects, while uncovering a hierarchical, task-dependent organization of different biological information across model layers. By further systematically training and evaluating a broad panel of model variants spanning model capacity, training duration and dataset size, we uncover distinct scaling behaviors across structural, evolutionary and functional capabilities. Together, these findings establish LIMBER as a versatile RNA foundation model and provide broader insights into how architectural design, internal representations and scaling shape the learning of RNA sequence-structure-function relationships.

title: Static Recovery Is Not Dynamic Stability: Dynamics-Aware Benchmarking of Protein Motif Scaffolding
authors: Emile de Bruyn; Moritz Schäffler; Jannik Schneider; Sebastian R. Schmidt; Chanwoong Hwang; Aleena Siji; Utkarsh Upadhyay; Stefan Bauer; Alexander Schug; Stefan Kesselheim; Artur Yakimovich; Alina Bazarova
abstract: Protein motif scaffolding benchmarks assess whether generative models can build scaffolds around functionally important residues. Their conclusions depend on which motifs are tested and which criteria define success. Existing benchmarks typically use small hand-curated motif sets and static refolding criteria, but protein function often depends on conformational ensembles and transitions. Here, we address both benchmark scope and success criteria. We introduce BILBY-PRO, a systematically derived benchmark of structurally conserved functional motifs from PROSITE-linked experimental structures, comprising 220 cases from 174 PROSITE motif-pattern entries. Evaluating six recent scaffold-generation models reveals distinct patterns in target coverage and unique-solution yield: RFDiffusion and Proteina solve more targets, whereas ESM3 produces more unique successful scaffolds on the targets it solves. We further introduce BILBY-MD, a reference-based all-atom molecular dynamics evaluation framework. Applied to statically solved designs from the original MotifBench benchmark, it compares motif drift, scaffold drift, motif-contact preservation, and motif-dihedral free-energy landscapes against reference simulations. Of 55 statically solved model-problem pairs, 31 satisfy our MD-supported criterion and only 8 pass all checks. Compact, self-contained motifs are often MD-supported, whereas interface-like or context-dependent motifs fail more frequently. Static refolding success therefore provides useful evidence of local motif recovery but does not establish dynamical fidelity of the full scaffold. BILBY highlights three complementary axes of motif-scaffolding evaluation: target coverage, unique-solution yield, and MD-supported dynamical fidelity.

title: A hierarchy of physics-embedded neural operators for structural dynamic surrogate modelingA hierarchy of physics-embedded neural operators for structural dynamic surrogate modeling
authors: Amir Ansrollahi; Mehmet Sefa Orak
abstract: Structural-response surrogates must capture moving resonances, phase changes, and unequal-amplitude transfer channels during optimization or health-state changes. Physics-embedded learning seeks FEA-level accuracy at lower cost by embedding physics in inputs, forward passes, losses, and backpropagation. We propose Modal Rational (MR), mapping structural features to modal quantities for analytical frequency-response reconstruction. The Physics-Guided Modal Operator Network (PGMON) adds bounded frequency, damping, and residual-flexibility corrections. Modal Operator with Structural GELU and Anchored-SIREN Correction (MOSAIC) denotes the bounded spectral-discrepancy framework used here; MOSAIC-MR and MOSAIC-PGMON add such discrepancies. They support finite-dimensional maps and physical decoders for future neural operators; evidence is fixed-topology, not a completed operator comparison. Two 20,000-design populations are studied: an 80 m steel truss tower with variable member areas and attached masses, and a tapered shell beam with ten variable station masses. Archived tests cover ten designs and seven acceleration histories per structure; they are benchmarks, not seismic-design assessments. With 5% reference modal damping, MR, PGMON, and MOSAIC give mean displacement-history errors of 0.73-0.76% for the tower and 0.029-0.116% for the beam, against declared band-limited modal references. Supplied modal frequencies are distinguished from design-only use; unequal parameter counts and training settings are explicit. Error analysis separates learned modal discrepancies, truncation, and excitation weighting, explaining acceleration and difficult-tower limits and risks of blind use. Results support physically structured prediction but limit claims about generalization, computational savings, and added corrections. Next is developing and validating neural operators around these architectures.

title: Discrete Backbone Elasticity and Curvature-Dependent Torsion Statistics in Proteins
authors: Yiquan Wang; Mingyu Bian; Jiayuan Ma
abstract: Coarse-grained models of protein conformational dynamics use $\mathrm{C}_α$ geometry to describe the probabilities of regular helices, ordered turns and disordered conformations. To test how much of this order arises from local chain elasticity, we connect discrete Hasimoto frame transport to neighboring bending mismatch, deriving a curvature-product torsion interaction and a six-parameter generalized von Mises density. Fitted on 194 chains from the ATLAS molecular dynamics database and tested on 1744 sequence-nonredundant proteins, this baseline reduces negative log-density loss from 1.490 to 1.160 nats, torsion-sign error from 12.26 to 2.15 percentage points, and helix-fraction error from 21.84 to 10.41 points. Ablations and circular-moment projections against reference generative models motivate extensions to anisotropic stiffness and two partition-function-weighted elastic states, further lowering test loss to 0.790 nats and helix error to 1.65 points. The fixed hierarchy also improves predictions across 72 trajectories of peptides $\mathrm{Fs}$ and $(\mathrm{AAQAA})_3$ and miniprotein $\mathrm{HP35}$ spanning varied starting conformations and force fields. Remaining angular errors in these trajectories are associated with atomic context at shared bends, as bend-matched peptide frames adopt opposite torsion signs with distinct hydrogen-bond patterns and a proline-containing $\mathrm{HP35}$ turn remains at negative torsion. Introducing a bilinearly coupled $\mathrm{C}_α$--$\mathrm{N}$ orientation angle largely reparameterizes the existing bend-dependent harmonics, with an empirical $L^2$ Gram projection placing 96.7\% to 99.6\% of its added coefficient-function squared norm within the original six-function span. These results link discrete Hasimoto elasticity to statistical backbone potentials and clarify the scope and limits of local $\mathrm{C}_α$ geometry.

title: Learning Noise Optimization for Reward Alignment in Few-Step Generative Models
authors: Hongeun Kim; Jeongsol Kim; Jong Chul Ye
abstract: Reward alignment for diffusion- and flow-based generative models is often formulated over stochastic trajectories, making it less suitable for few-step deterministic generators. Initial noise optimization provides a trajectory-free alternative, but existing gradient-free methods require costly per-sample search at inference. We introduce LeNO (Learning Noise Optimization), which amortizes reward-guided initial noise optimization into a learned residual transport while keeping the pretrained generator frozen. LeNO learns an anchor-conditioned distribution over noise corrections using Local GRPO and scalar rewards, eliminating iterative test-time optimization. For Gaussian initial noise with norm-preserving projection, we derive a tractable upper bound on the KL divergence between the corrected noise distribution and the original prior, providing a principled regularization objective. We evaluate LeNO on few-step text-to-image and protein structure generation, including expensive black-box designability rewards. Across both domains, LeNO improves target rewards with a single noise correction at inference while largely preserving generation quality and diversity.

title: Empirical Bayes Flow Matching for Continuous Cryo-EM Heterogeneity
authors: Daniel Aibinder; Azmi Haider; Dan Rosenbaum
abstract: We address the problem of learning generative priors over high-dimensional latent variables from indirect, noisy observations, with a focus on continuous heterogeneity in cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). In this setting, 3D atomic structures $x \in \mathbb{R}^{3N_a}$ are never directly observed and must be inferred from 2D projection images $y$ generated by a complex, non-linear forward operator. We propose Empirical Bayes Flow Matching (EB-FM), a method that learns a flow matching prior $p_θ(x)$ directly from observations using a Monte Carlo stochastic approximation Expectation-Maximization framework. EB-FM alternates between an E-step that performs approximate posterior sampling from $p_θ(x \mid y)$ via guided flow-based generation while maintaining persistent latent estimates through stochastic approximation, and an M-step that updates the flow model using these stabilized latent variables as training targets. This approach eliminates the need for pretraining on clean data and naturally accommodates non-linear forward models. We validate our method on controlled inverse problems using two-moons and MNIST data, and demonstrate its effectiveness on simulated cryo-EM data with known poses, showing that EB-FM can recover continuous distributions of protein conformations directly in atomic-coordinate space.

title: Ablating Design Choices for Protein Ensemble Generators Across Structural Regimes
authors: Eoin Quinn; Oliver Bent
abstract: Generative models of protein conformational ensembles inherit much of their design from structure prediction for folded proteins. Ordered and disordered proteins, however, occupy distinct structural regimes, and we investigate how design choices hold up across them. Using a minimal C$α$ flow-matching model, we ablate choices of architecture, sequence conditioning, rigid-body alignment and training source, and evaluate each variant against experimental SAXS and NMR chemical-shift data partitioned into ordered, disordered, multi-domain and transitional proteins. Mixture-of-experts routing, a static pair representation and a disorder probe have no detectable effect, a smaller protein language model performs worse on ordered proteins but not on disordered ones, and alignment in the loss degrades agreement with SAXS. Replacing coarse-grained simulations of disordered proteins with fragment-assembled ensembles improves agreement with chemical shifts at a cost to SAXS, while an equal mixture of the two keeps most of the gain at a smaller cost. This points to the training data, rather than the architecture, as the main constraint.

title: Predicting protein structures at any folding stage from sequence
authors: Lisheng Zhang; Qingsong Li; Zinan Xie; Yanting Yang; Qikui Yang; Peng Lu; Zhican Fu; Wentao Cui; Runtong Hou; Zhengwei Xie
abstract: Protein structure prediction has largely focused on native conformations, leaving the continuum of unfolded states, folding intermediates, and native structures difficult to access. We present FoldScape, a sequence-conditioned deep learning framework for generating protein conformational ensembles at specified folding fractions $Q$. Trained on approximately one million conformations from 10,000 protein sequences, FoldScape combines coarse-grained folding and all-atom mechanical-unfolding trajectories. It reconstructs three-dimensional $C_α$ chains through hierarchical sliding-window regressions of inter-residue distances, chain-level assembly, and a rectified-flow decoder. By conditioning on folding progress, FoldScape generates conformations from unfolded states through intermediates to native-state structures without protein-specific molecular dynamics at inference. In matched-sample comparisons, FoldScape achieves median conformational-space coverage of 0.989, 0.722, and 0.877 along radius of gyration, fraction of native contacts $Q$, and secondary-structure fraction, respectively, versus 0.05, 0.05, and 0.10 for seed-varied AlphaFold 3 ensembles. Coverage advantages are consistent across the evaluated proteins and robust to binning choices. Reconstruction accuracy remains approximately stable across the evaluated stages of a folding trajectory, and stride-one crop-and-superpose inference extends predictions to chains several times longer than the single-pass limit. Analyses of mechanical-unfolding trajectories show residue-resolved pathways, reproducible extension-conditioned observables across pulling velocities, and geometrically coherent segments in partially unfolded chains. FoldScape extends sequence-based structure prediction beyond a single folded endpoint to controllable conformational-ensemble generation across protein folding.

title: Evaluation Contracts and Evaluation Leverage: Sliced-Gap Readings in Structured Prediction Can Move Without Model Change
authors: Hao Lu; Weixing Zhu; Ruiyang Li
abstract: NLP evaluation reports routinely cite sliced performance differences, most prominently the intra-inter gap in document-level relation extraction, as capability evidence. We show that such gap readings are joint properties of models and evaluation contracts: scoring function, gold version, threshold, output format, and prompt language. With predictions frozen, a method ordering reverses under a gold-standard exchange (+0.0363, CI excluding zero; tie-level after), movement localizing where gold re-partitions: renames are gauge transformations (Delta=0; re-annotation +0.862). We formalize this as an evaluation leverage account centered on the rank-flip condition. Constructively, the audited evaluation reading (AER) is a contract-marginalized, tie-declared, seed-prescribed, gate-filtered procedure whose tie declarations cover every contract-induced flip on the declared WMT19 grids (14/14; held-out 73% vs. union-of-ties 89%), matching the best single metric contract at epsilon=0.10 equivalence. Evidence spans DocRE, HacRED, a UD probe, and released gold revisions; an alternative-reference-set replication extends it beyond our testbeds. Failed predictions retained as boundaries; a 5% violation gate flags unverifiable settings and bounds survivor-selection bias. We release EvalLever, a preregistered workflow with an amendment trail; on LLM-as-judge grids, the audited ensemble stabilizes every unstable pair (13-15 to zero; generic ensemble shrinkage: the preregistered correlation criterion failed, the companion stabilization criterion passed).

title: ProteoCraft: Protein Design as Proposal-Verification Search
authors: Fang Wu; Hongbin Lin; Bingchen Duan; Yuchen Wang; Li Erran Li; Yanjie Huang; Mingxuan Cao; Yijun Ma; Yunxiang Mo; Yanchao Li; Kuan Pang; Juangui Xu; Hanqun Cao; Dongwei Jiang; Xinyue Xu; Xiangru Tang; Zehong Wang; Jian Ma; Kejun Ying; Guanlue Li; Mingran Cao; Fanjin Wang; Tianfan Fu; Shuangjia Zheng; Yao Shu; Jure Leskovec; Yejin Choi
abstract: Protein-protein interactions underpin nearly all biological processes. Yet, designing proteins with desired interactions remains challenging due to the structural complexity governing molecular recognition. This study views protein design as a search optimization problem over a combinatorial sequence space under expensive structural evaluation. Toward this goal, we introduce a novel tree-based search framework, ProteoCraft, that employs approximate structural gradients from diffusion-based structure predictors as effective proposal policies to specify where the search should explore. Complete no-gradient inference of folding models separately assigns values to the resulting sequences, determining what is good. ProteoCraft allocates this verification budget through a coarse-to-fine paradigm: multi-site edits first explore distinct sequence basins, then verified promising states undergo strict single-site refinement. Across fourteen de novo binder-design settings spanning eight target proteins, five immune-relevant TCR-facing targets, and four localized CDR redesign tasks, ProteoCraft improves design quality and high-confidence yield. These improvements persist under independent AF2-IG and Rosetta-based interface evaluation. Prospective experimental validation further yielded an 82.9% binding hit rate for PD-L1 miniproteins, with a best measured KD of 0.879 nM, and confirmed binding of designed IFNAR2 VHH. Our code is available at https://github.com/smiles724/ProteoCraft_v1.

title: BEND 2.0: Benchmarking the Capabilities Needed to Design DNA
authors: Andreas Bjerregaard; Rachael DeVries; Dionysia Danai Brilli; Panagiotis Antoniadis; Yan Li; Anders Krogh; Wouter Boomsma; Ole Winther; Frederikke Isa Marin
abstract: Genomic foundation models are increasingly used to propose DNA sequences and edits. But successful design requires capabilities that current benchmarks do not measure. Here we introduce BEND 2.0 (BENchmark for DNA language models), which tests how well models predict the effects of DNA changes and whether these predictions can guide sequence design. Across eight tasks built on five experimental datasets, we find that model choice and how representations are accessed both affect performance. Linear readouts fitted to frozen representations can match or exceed models' native outputs, and functional post-training substantially improves the models' capabilities. Linear readouts transfer well across experimental assays and genes, suggesting that models capture functional patterns beyond the data used to fit individual predictors. At the same time, strong prediction of average effects can conceal weaker prediction of context-specific effects, and accurate prediction of combined mutation effects does not imply accurate prediction of their interactions. In design tasks, model predictions can reduce the number of candidates needed to find a desired response, but still leave substantial room for better design choices, particularly for context-specific and multi-cell objectives. Our benchmark reveals that genomic models now display signs of general utility but have yet to saturate on performance in even simple tasks.

title: Auto-Research Agent on MSA Organization to Improve Protein-Protein Complex Structure Prediction
authors: Zilu Zhang; Jing Bao; Lifeng Qiao; Sheng Xu; Qiantai Feng; Siqi Sun; Yang Yang
abstract: Protein-complex structure prediction with AlphaFold 3 depends on MSA content, depth, and cross-chain pairing. Current pipelines apply uniform recipes, typically maximizing depth and pairing by species, yet even whether cross-chain pairing helps AF3 remains contested. We show that the value of both depth and pairing is strongly target-dependent, so no single recipe is optimal across interfaces. We introduce an autonomous agent that treats a frozen AF3 as a black-box experimental instrument. For each target, the agent formulates biological hypotheses, analyzes and reorganizes the MSA, and iteratively refines sequence selection and pairing using predictor label-free signals alone. On 1{,}015 protein--protein interfaces from three benchmarks released after AF3's training cutoff, the agent improves overall interface DockQ over AF3's default pipeline and fixed MSA recipes on every benchmark, while using on average 60\% fewer MSA sequences than the default. Gains are largest for inter-species heteromers, where species-based pairing is unreliable: mean DockQ increases from 0.465 to 0.612 on FoldBench and from 0.482 to 0.562 on HD439. The improvements arise from both sequence construction and pairing policy, including deliberate non-pairing. These results recast MSA design as a target-specific problem and show that an autonomous agent can adapt it at test time through biological reasoning and self-directed, confidence-guided experimentation.

title: Visual-to-Executable Procedural Reconstruction of Buildings
authors: Zichong Zhu; Zhihao Liu; Andrei Sharf; Zhanglin Cheng
abstract: Procedural modeling offers compact, editable, and reusable representations for architectural content, but building such models still depends heavily on manually authored grammars. We study image-based procedural building reconstruction from in-the-wild images, with the goal of recovering an executable procedural description that can be instantiated as an editable 3D building asset. Because a single image provides only partial and view-dependent evidence, we focus on recovering the dominant visible facade(s) and attach the recovered facade program to a simple mass model for building-level instantiation. Our method decomposes this task into two structured prediction stages. First, a Global Structure Layout Tree recovers facade-scale split-and-repeat organization through a fine-tuned layout model with render-guided visual-symbolic reflection. Second, a Component Parameterization schema maps representative facade tiles to structured procedural attributes for local architectural component synthesis. These two representations are then deterministically compiled into executable Computer Generated Architecture (CGA) programs, avoiding the brittleness of direct low-level program generation. Experiments show that the proposed framework handles both regular facades and challenging in-the-wild images, while maintaining high structural consistency, procedural executability, and fine-grained architectural detail. The recovered programs further enable controllable and reusable 3D building asset generation.

title: Molecular Curvature Enables Tubular π-Stacked Pathways in Three-Dimensional Conductive Metal-Organic Frameworks
authors: Weishan Li; Jia-Xiang Zhang; Tongyang Zhao; Hao Chen; Tianyang Chen; Ze-Fan Yao; Jin-Hu Dou
abstract: Conductive metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) are commonly constructed from planar aromatic ligands, whose geometries favor conventional π-stacking arrangements. However, intrinsically twisted ligands offer an alternative geometric approach to directing aromatic packing and constructing unconventional framework architectures. Here, we employ intrinsically twisted, butterfly-shaped dibenzo[g,p]chrysene-2,3,6,7,10,11,14,15-octaol (DBC) ligands to construct a series of lanthanide MOFs. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction reveals an interpenetrated three-dimensional framework in which π-π interactions between the aromatic fragments generate axially extended tubular π-stacked pathways, alongside one-dimensional channels rich in hydrogen-bonding sites. Lanthanide substitution preserves the overall tubular framework topology while modulating aromatic stacking distances and local pore environments. PrDBC single crystals exhibit mixed electron-proton transport, with electron and proton conductivities reaching 1.62 x 10-3 and 4.37 x 10-4 S cm-1, respectively, at 338 K and 30% relative humidity. This work highlights molecular curvature as a structural design strategy for constructing three-dimensional conductive MOFs that integrate tubular aromatic stacks with tunable pore environments for mixed electron-proton transport.

title: Site-orbit masked twin-branch Transformer for symmetry-constrained crystal generation
authors: Junchi Liu; Haoran Si; Luo Yan; Sergei Tretiak; Liujiang Zhou
abstract: Generative models for crystal structure prediction (CSP) have expanded the search space for novel materials and improved screening efficiency. However, simultaneously generating stable and novel structures remains challenging because of the complex structural and physical constraints governing crystals. To address this challenge, we propose site-orbit masked twin-branch Transformer model (ST2M), a symmetry-guided discrete--continuous diffusion framework incorporating degree-of-freedom masks and conditioned on Wyckoff patterns. ST2M represents crystal structures as sequences of independent occupied Wyckoff orbits and employs a twin-branch Transformer to jointly denoise discrete and continuous variables. In our experiments, ST2M achieves a structural validity of 96.37\%. For known patterns in dataset, 23.86\% of generated structures simultaneously satisfy stability, uniqueness, and novelty criteria, representing a relative improvement of 68.15\% over the best-performing baseline. First-principles calculations identify a total of 21 previously unreported stable structures among selected candidates with low predicted energies. These results demonstrate that ST2M can generate chemically viable crystal candidates under prescribed crystallographic constraints and generalize to unknown Wyckoff patterns, providing a practical route to accelerated materials discovery.

title: Graphs Have Structure: Declarative Manifolds, 3D Z-Order Monoid Roll-ups, and Zero-Simulation Visual Analytics in a Graph DBMS
authors: Madhulatha Mandarapu; Sandeep Kunkunuru
abstract: Every real-world graph is embedded in an ambient structural manifold: proteins fold in Euclidean space ($R^3$), telecom networks sit on a planetary surface ($S^2 \times R$), and ontologies and calendars form discrete subsumption posets ($(V, \sqsubseteq)$). Yet property graph databases treat node coordinates as opaque payload scalars, leave spatial proximity edges unindexed, and force visualizers into $O(V^2)$ client-side force-directed simulations that destroy true geometry and truncate hierarchy roll-ups. We elevate ambient manifold structure to a first-class primitive in Samyama Graph. First, we introduce a declarative and auto-detected structural convention contract (samyama.structure/1) persisted in .sgsnap headers that binds node labels to Euclidean 3D, Geo-Spherical, Causal Spacetime, or Poset Hierarchy manifolds. Second, we show that both discrete posets (via Order-Embedded Hierarchy $[tin, tout]$ DFS intervals) and continuous 3D manifolds (via a 63-bit 3D Morton Z-order Structural-Geometric Index, SGI) reduce regional aggregation to 1D rank-interval monoid folds answered directly from index-resident Fenwick trees (SUM, COUNT) and Segment Trees (MIN, MAX). At $100,000$ 3D nodes, SGI builds in $28.14$ ms and answers Morton-interval SUM and MAX roll-ups in $0.048\,μ$s and $0.104\,μ$s---$8,345.1\times$ and $3,824.4\times$ faster than property scans. Third, we introduce 3D voxel-hashed virtual contact edges weighted by Topological--Geometric Stress $σ(u,v) = d_{graph}(u,v) / d_{manifold}(u,v)$ to isolate long-range tertiary folds, plus manifold-guided $A^*$ shortest-path search that cuts explored states by up to $3.80\times$ over Dijkstra. Fourth, we replace client layout simulation with server-computed 3D Cone-Tree/Ribbon coordinates and a non-WebGL 2.5D Isometric projection with painter's-order depth sorting and sub-millisecond Level-of-Detail (LoD) macro-cuts.
